relevance_reason: Only the title of an Author Correction notice is available. It contains no patient, variant, functional or other data that a curator could cite in the colorectal cancer entry.
Reports germline FAN1 mutations as a cause of hereditary MMR-proficient colorectal cancer in families meeting the Amsterdam criteria.

findings.statement: Seguí et al. (2015) performed exome sequencing on 3 members of a family with colorectal cancer that met the Amsterdam criteria for hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer and had mismatch repair-proficient tumors. All 3 carried a nonsense variant in FAN1, which encodes a nuclease involved in DNA interstrand cross-link repair.
quotes: We performed exome sequencing of DNA from 3 individuals from a family with colorectal cancer who met the Amsterdam criteria for risk of hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer.

These individuals had mismatch repair-proficient tumors and each carried nonsense variant in the FANCD2/FANCI-associated nuclease 1 gene (FAN1), which encodes a nuclease involved in DNA inter-strand cross-link repair.

findings.statement: Seguí et al. (2015) sequenced FAN1 in 176 additional families with a history of colorectal cancer and performed in vitro functional analyses of the mutant FAN1 proteins found. FAN1 mutations were detected in about 3% of families that met the Amsterdam criteria and had mismatch repair-proficient cancers with no previously associated mutations. The authors concluded that these findings link colorectal cancer predisposition to the Fanconi anemia DNA repair pathway.
quotes: We sequenced FAN1 in 176 additional families with histories of colorectal cancer and performed in vitro functional analyses of the mutant forms of FAN1 identified.
We detected FAN1 mutations in approximately 3% of families who met the Amsterdam criteria and had mismatch repair-proficient cancers with no previously associated mutations.
These findings link colorectal cancer predisposition to the Fanconi anemia DNA repair pathway, supporting the connection between genome integrity and cancer risk.

relevance_reason: This is a trial analysis showing that somatic RAS mutations beyond KRAS exon 2 (in KRAS exons 3 and 4 and NRAS) predict no benefit from panitumumab in metastatic colorectal cancer, and that BRAF mutations carry a poor prognosis. It informs the molecular genetics and treatment sections of the entry.

findings.statement: In a prospective-retrospective analysis of the PRIME trial, Douillard et al. (2013) tested tumors from 639 patients with metastatic colorectal cancer that had no KRAS exon 2 mutations. The tumors were tested for mutations in KRAS exons 3 and 4, NRAS exons 2, 3, and 4, and BRAF exon 15. A total of 108 patients (17%) with nonmutated KRAS exon 2 had other RAS mutations. These mutations were associated with inferior progression-free and overall survival with panitumumab-FOLFOX4, consistent with findings in patients with KRAS exon 2 mutations.
quotes: A total of 639 patients who had metastatic colorectal cancer without KRAS mutations in exon 2 had results for at least one of the following: KRAS exon 3 or 4; NRAS exon 2, 3, or 4; or BRAF exon 15.
A total of 108 patients (17%) with nonmutated KRAS exon 2 had other RAS mutations.

These mutations were associated with inferior progression-free survival and overall survival with panitumumab-FOLFOX4 treatment, which was consistent with the findings in patients with KRAS mutations in exon 2.

findings.statement: Douillard et al. (2013) found that among 512 patients with metastatic colorectal cancer without RAS mutations, panitumumab-FOLFOX4 improved progression-free survival compared with FOLFOX4 alone (10.1 vs 7.9 months; hazard ratio 0.72; P = 0.004). It also improved overall survival (26.0 vs 20.2 months; hazard ratio 0.78; P = 0.04). The authors concluded that additional RAS mutations predicted a lack of response to panitumumab-FOLFOX4.
quotes: Among 512 patients without RAS mutations, progression-free survival was 10.1 months with panitumumab-FOLFOX4 versus 7.9 months with FOLFOX4 alone (hazard ratio for progression or death with combination therapy, 0.72; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.58 to 0.90; P=0.004).
Overall survival was 26.0 months in the panitumumab-FOLFOX4 group versus 20.2 months in the FOLFOX4-alone group (hazard ratio for death, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.62 to 0.99; P=0.04).
Additional RAS mutations predicted a lack of response in patients who received panitumumab-FOLFOX4.

findings.statement: Douillard et al. (2013) found that BRAF mutations were a negative prognostic factor in patients with metastatic colorectal cancer.
quotes: BRAF mutations were a negative prognostic factor.

relevance_reason: Review abstract on genomics and epigenomics of colorectal cancer; gives general context only, with no new patients, variants or experiments.

findings.statement: In a review, Schweiger et al. (2013) described colorectal cancer as a complex disease with several layers, involving both the genome and the epigenome, with direct effects on gene and microRNA expression signatures. They noted that many tumor-suppressor genes and oncogenes are frequently mutated in colorectal cancer and might drive the malignant transformation.
quotes: We show that colorectal cancer is a multilayer complex disease affecting the genome as well as the epigenome with direct consequences on the gene and microRNA (miRNA) expression signatures.
Work over the last decades has uncovered a number of tumor-suppressor and oncogenes which are frequently mutated and might thus be responsible for the malignant transformation.

relevance_reason: Large somatic genomic study of primary colon tumours. It reports recurrent RSPO2 and RSPO3 fusions, newly identified recurrent mutated genes and copy-number changes, with functional and mouse-model support. This is somatic evidence relevant to colorectal cancer.

findings.statement: Seshagiri et al. (2012) sequenced the exomes of 72 primary colon tumour-normal pairs (15 MSI, 57 MSS) and also analysed RNA-seq, SNP-array and whole-genome data. They identified 36,303 protein-altering somatic changes. In MSS tumours they found 23 significantly mutated genes. These included known genes (KRAS, APC, TP53, SMAD4, FBXW7, PIK3CA) and new ones such as the checkpoint kinase gene ATM. They also found new recurrent mutations in TCF7L2, in TET2 and TET3, and in ERBB3.
quotes: We have identified 36,303 protein-altering somatic changes that include several new recurrent mutations in the Wnt pathway gene TCF7L2, chromatin-remodelling genes such as TET2 and TET3 and receptor tyrosine kinases including ERBB3.
The MSS CRC genes identified from this analysis included previously reported genes such as KRAS, APC, TP53, SMAD4, FBXW7 and PIK3CA and several new genes including the cell cycle checkpoint gene ATM

findings.statement: Seshagiri et al. (2012) found TCF12 mutations in 5 MSI colon tumours. Three of the 5 mutations hit a hotspot at Arg603 in the helix-loop-helix domain, and the authors stated that these probably abolish DNA binding. ERBB3 was mutated in 6 of 72 tumours (8%), and all three TET genes (TET1, TET2, TET3) were mutated.
quotes: TCF12, a CRC gene identified in a mouse model screen, was mutated in five of the MSI samples. A hotspot mutation in TCF12 at Arg 603 (three out of five mutations) was found within the TCF12 helix–loop–helix domain and probably abolishes its DNA-binding ability
ERBB3, which was mutated in 8% (6 out of 72) of the samples, contained multiple hotspot mutations that were oncogenic

findings.statement: In 74 tumour-normal pairs, Seshagiri et al. (2012) found IGF2 overexpression in 8 of 68 colon tumours (12%), and 7 of these 8 had focal amplification of the IGF2 locus. They also found KRAS amplification (10 of 74) and MYC amplification (17 of 74). Deletions involved FHIT (22 of 74), APC, PTEN and SMAD3. Chromosome 18q (carrying SMAD4 and SMAD2) was frequently lost and chromosome 20q was frequently gained.
quotes: we also identified IGF2 upregulation in 12% (8 out of 68) of the samples
Most (7 out of 8) of the tumours with IGF2 overexpression also showed focal amplification of the IGF2 locus
Deletion involving FHIT, a tumour-suppressor gene, was observed in 30% (22 out of 74) of the samples

findings.statement: Using RNA-seq, Seshagiri et al. (2012) found a recurrent EIF3E(exon 1)-RSPO2(exon 2) fusion in 2 of 68 MSS colon tumours (3%). The fusion is expected to produce functional RSPO2 driven by the EIF3E promoter. Whole-genome sequencing showed a 158-kb deletion in one tumour and a 113-kb deletion in the other, each placing EIF3E exon 1 next to the 5-prime end of RSPO2. RSPO2 expression was elevated in the fusion-positive tumours.
quotes: The recurrent RSPO2 fusion identified in two tumour samples involves EIF3E exon 1 and RSPO2 exon 2 (Fig. 3b). This fusion transcript is expected to produce a functional RSPO2 protein driven by the EIF3E promoter
identified a 158 kilobases (kb) deletion in one sample and a 113 kb deletion in the second sample, both of which places exon 1 of EIF3E in close proximity to the 5′ end of RSPO2

findings.statement: Seshagiri et al. (2012) found PTPRK-RSPO3 fusions in 5 of 68 colon tumours (8%), caused by simple or complex inversions on chromosome 6q. In 4 tumours the in-frame PTPRK(e1)-RSPO3(e2) fusion keeps the entire RSPO3 coding sequence but uses the PTPRK secretion signal in place of RSPO3's own. In 1 tumour the in-frame PTPRK(e7)-RSPO3(e2) fusion encodes a protein of about 70 kD made of PTPRK amino acids 1-387 joined to RSPO3 amino acids 34-272.
quotes: The RSPO3 gene fusions were observed in 5 out of 68 tumours and involve PTPRK as the 5′ partner.
The PTPRK(e1)–RSPO3(e2) transcript found in four samples is an in-frame fusion that preserves the entire coding sequence of RSPO3 and replaces its secretion signal sequence with that of PTPRK
The PTPRK(e7)–RSPO3(e2) fusion, detected in one sample, is also an in-frame fusion that encodes a ∼70 kDa protein consisting of the first 387 amino acids of PTPRK

findings.statement: Seshagiri et al. (2012) found that the RSPO2 and RSPO3 fusions were mutually exclusive with each other. The fusions occurred in tumours without APC mutation or copy loss (P = 0.038), except for one RSPO2-fusion tumour with a single APC allele, and they were also mutually exclusive with CTNNB1 mutations. Every fusion-positive tumour carried a KRAS or BRAF mutation. Fusion-positive tumours showed upregulation of Wnt target genes similar to APC-mutant tumours, which the authors suggested means the fusions act analogously to APC mutations.
quotes: the RSPO2 and RSPO3 fusions were mutually exclusive and occurred in tumours that did not contain APC mutations or copy loss (Fig. 4d; P = 0.038, Fisher's exact test)

the RSPO gene fusions were mutually exclusive with mutations in CTNNB1, another Wnt pathway gene that is mutated in CRC. However, all the samples with RSPO gene fusions also carried a mutation in either KRAS or BRAF

findings.statement: Seshagiri et al. (2012) expressed the RSPO fusion constructs in 293T cells and showed that the fusion proteins were secreted. In a TOPbrite luciferase reporter assay, conditioned media containing the fusion proteins activated Wnt signalling, and this effect was further potentiated by added Wnt. The same activity was seen in HT-29 colon cancer cells. The authors concluded that R-spondins probably act as drivers in human colorectal cancer.
quotes: As observed with wild-type RSPO2 and RSPO3, conditioned media from cells transfected with RSPO fusion expression constructs led to activation of the Wnt pathway (Fig. 4b).
Taken together, our findings indicate that the R-spondins probably function as drivers in human CRCs.

findings.statement: Seshagiri et al. (2012) reported that Rspo2 was a top candidate cancer gene in Sleeping Beauty transposon mutagenesis screens in mouse models of colorectal cancer. In these mouse tumours, transposon insertions in Apc and in Rspo2 were mostly mutually exclusive. One tumour with an insertion near the Rspo2 transcription start site had about 20-fold higher Rspo2 mRNA than adjacent normal tissue.
quotes: transposon-based insertional mutagenesis screens in mouse models of CRC identified Rspo2 as a top-candidate cancer gene
analysis of these mouse colon tumours showed that the transposon insertions were in most cases mutually exclusive between Apc and Rspo2
we found a ∼ 20-fold increase in Rspo2 messenger RNA expression in a mouse tumour carrying a transposon insertion near the Rspo2 transcription start site

relevance_reason: Large-scale genomic characterization of somatic alterations in colorectal carcinoma, directly informing the molecular genetics of CRC.

findings.statement: The Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012) performed a genome-scale analysis of 276 colorectal carcinoma samples, including exome sequencing of 224 tumor-normal pairs, DNA copy number, promoter methylation, and mRNA and microRNA expression, with low-depth whole-genome sequencing of 97 samples. Overall, 16% of tumors were hypermutated; three-quarters of these had high microsatellite instability (MSI-H), usually with hypermethylation and MLH1 silencing, and one-quarter had somatic mismatch-repair gene and POLE mutations.
quotes: To characterize somatic alterations in colorectal carcinoma, we conducted a genome-scale analysis of 276 samples, analysing exome sequence, DNA copy number, promoter methylation and messenger RNA and microRNA expression.

In total, 16% of colorectal carcinomas were found to be hypermutated: three-quarters of these had the expected high microsatellite instability, usually with hypermethylation and MLH1 silencing, and one-quarter had somatic mismatch-repair gene and polymerase ε (POLE) mutations.

findings.statement: Among 30 hypermutated tumors with complete data, the Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012) found that 23 (77%) were MSI-H, including 19 with MLH1 methylation (17 with CIMP); the remaining 7, including the 6 with the highest mutation rates, lacked MSI-H, CIMP, or MLH1 methylation but usually had somatic mutations in mismatch-repair genes or POLE aberrations.
quotes: Among the 30 hypermutated tumours with a complete data set, 23 (77%) had high levels of MSI (MSI-H). Included in this group were 19 tumours with MLH1 methylation, 17 of which had CIMP.

the remaining seven hypermutated tumours, including the six with the highest mutation rates, lacked MSI-H, CIMP or MLH1 methylation but usually had somatic mutations in one or more mismatch-repair genes or POLΕ aberrations

findings.statement: The Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012) identified 24 significantly mutated genes; among non-hypermutated tumors the most frequently mutated were APC, TP53, KRAS, PIK3CA, FBXW7, SMAD4, TCF7L2, and NRAS, with CTNNB1, SMAD2, FAM123B (WTX), and SOX9 also frequently mutated. All 9 SOX9 mutant alleles in non-hypermutated tumors were frameshift or nonsense, and ATM and ARID1A had a disproportionate number of frameshift or nonsense mutations.
quotes: Twenty-four genes were significantly mutated, and in addition to the expected APC, TP53, SMAD4, PIK3CA and KRAS mutations, we found frequent mutations in ARID1A, SOX9 and FAM123B.
Among the non-hypermutated tumours, the eight most frequently mutated genes were APC, TP53, KRAS, PIK3CA, FBXW7, SMAD4, TCF7L2 and NRAS.

Mutations in SOX9, a gene important for cell differentiation in the intestinal stem cell niche,, have not been associated previously with human cancer, but all nine mutated alleles in the non-hypermutated CRCs were frameshift or nonsense mutations.

findings.statement: In hypermutated tumors, the Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012) found frequent mutations in ACVR2A, APC, TGFBR2, MSH3, MSH6, SLC9A9, and TCF7L2, along with mostly BRAF V600E mutations; TP53 (60% vs 20%) and APC (81% vs 51%) were significantly less frequently mutated in hypermutated than non-hypermutated tumors, indicating that the two groups progress through different sequences of genetic events.
quotes: In the hypermutated tumours, ACVR2A, APC, TGFBR2, MSH3, MSH6, SLC9A9 and TCF7L2 were frequent targets of mutation (Fig. 1b), along with mostly BRAF(V600E) mutations.
TP53 (60 versus 20%, P < 0.0001) and APC (81% versus 51%, P = 0.0023; both Fisher’s exact test)
These findings indicate that hypermutated and non-hypermutated tumours progress through different sequences of genetic events.

findings.statement: The Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012) found that, excluding hypermutated cancers, colon and rectal carcinomas had indistinguishable patterns of copy number, CIMP, mRNA, and miRNA changes; however, tumors from the right/ascending colon were more likely to be hypermethylated and hypermutated, with three-quarters of hypermutated samples from the right colon.
quotes: Among the non-hypermutated tumours, however, the overall patterns of changes in copy number, CIMP, mRNA and miRNA were indistinguishable between colon and rectal carcinomas (Fig. 2).
Hypermethylation was more common in the right colon, and three-quarters of hypermutated samples came from the same site, although not all of them had MSI (Fig. 2).

findings.statement: Among 257 tumors profiled by SNP arrays, the Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012) found deletion of 18p and 18q (including SMAD4) in 66% and of 17p and 17q (including TP53) in 56%, 28 recurrent deletion peaks, and 17 regions of focal amplification, including an ERBB2-containing amplicon at 17q21.1 in 4% of tumors and a 100- to 150-kb amplification at 11p15.5 in 7% of tumors that included IGF2 and miR-483, whose expression was elevated.
quotes: Significantly deleted chromosome arms were 18p and q (including SMAD4) in 66% of the tumours and 17p and q (including TP53) in 56%.
An amplicon at 17q21.1, found in 4% of the tumours, contains seven genes, including the tyrosine kinase ERBB2.
One of the most common focal amplifications, found in 7% of the tumours, is the gain of a 100–150-kb region of the chromosome arm 11p15.5.

findings.statement: The Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012) found that IGF2 overexpression (by amplification or otherwise) was nearly mutually exclusive with PI3K pathway-activating events (PIK3CA, PIK3R1, PTEN), and that high IRS2 expression was mutually exclusive with IGF2 overexpression and PI3K pathway mutations, strongly suggesting that the IGF2-IGF1R-IRS2 axis signals to PI3K in CRC.
quotes: We found a pattern of near exclusivity (corrected P < 0.01) of IGF2 overexpression with genomic events known to activate the PI3K pathway (mutations of PIK3CA and PIK3R1 or deletion/mutation of PTEN; Fig. 3c and Supplementary Table 5).
These results strongly suggest that the IGF2–IGF1R–IRS2 axis signals to PI3K in CRC

findings.statement: By low-pass whole-genome sequencing of 97 tumors, the Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012) identified 3 cases in which the first 2 exons of NAV2 on chromosome 11 were fused to the 3-prime coding portion of TCF7L1 on chromosome 2, with the predicted fusion protein lacking the TCF3 beta-catenin-binding domain; 21 translocations involving TTC28 predicted its inactivation.
quotes: We found three separate cases in which the first two exons of the NAV2 gene on chromosome 11 are joined with the 3′ coding portion of TCF7L1 on chromosome 2 (Supplementary Fig. 5).
Intriguingly, in all three cases, the predicted structure of the NAV2–TCF7L1 fusion protein lacks the TCF3 β-catenin-binding domain.
We also observed 21 cases of translocation involving TTC28 located on chromosome 22 (Supplementary Table 6).

findings.statement: In integrated analysis of 195 tumors, the Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012) found WNT signaling altered in 93% of tumors, including biallelic APC inactivation or activating CTNNB1 mutations in about 80%, with FZD10 overexpressed in about 17%; 55% of non-hypermutated tumors had KRAS, NRAS, or BRAF alterations; TGF-beta pathway alterations occurred in 27% of non-hypermutated and 87% of hypermutated tumors; and TP53 was altered in 59% of non-hypermutated cases. PARADIGM analysis showed changes in MYC transcriptional targets in nearly 100% of tumors, suggesting an important role for MYC.
quotes: We found that the WNT signalling pathway was altered in 93% of all tumours, including biallelic inactivation of APC (Supplementary Table 7) or activating mutations of CTNNB1 in ∼80% of cases.
We found genomic alterations in TGFBR1, TGFBR2, ACVR2A, ACVR1B, SMAD2, SMAD3 and SMAD4 in 27% of the non-hypermutated and 87% of the hypermutated tumours.
nearly 100% of these tumours have changes in MYC transcriptional targets, both those promoted by and those inhibited by MYC.

findings.statement: The Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012) found mutations or amplifications of ERBB family genes in 13% of non-hypermutated and 53% of hypermutated cases, including recurrent ERBB2 V842I and ERBB3 V104M mutations in 4 and 2 non-hypermutated cases, respectively, and suggested these be evaluated as predictors of response to ERBB-targeted agents.
quotes: Mutations or amplifications in one of the four ERBB family genes are present in 22 out of 165 (13%) non-hypermutated and 16 out of 30 (53%) hypermutated cases.
Intriguingly, recurrent ERBB2(V842I) and ERBB3(V104M) mutations were found in four and two non-hypermutated cases, respectively.

findings.statement: The Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012) found molecular signatures associated with tumor aggressiveness, including somatic mutations in APC, TP53, PIK3CA, BRAF, and FBXW7; FBXW7 mutations (38 cases) and distant metastasis (32 cases) never co-occurred.
quotes: Association with tumour aggressiveness is also observed in altered expression of miRNAs and specific somatic mutations (APC, TP53, PIK3CA, BRAF and FBXW7; Supplementary Fig. 8b).
Mutations in FBXW7 (38 cases) and distant metastasis (32 cases) never co-occurred (P = 0.0019).

relevance_reason: Somatic KRAS mutations emerging in circulating tumor DNA as a mechanism of acquired resistance to anti-EGFR therapy (panitumumab) in metastatic colorectal cancer; relevant to molecular genetics/clinical management of CRC.

findings.statement: Diaz et al. (2012) retrospectively analyzed serial serum samples from 28 patients with chemorefractory metastatic colorectal cancer receiving panitumumab monotherapy for circulating mutant KRAS DNA. Of 24 patients whose tumors were initially KRAS wildtype, 9 (38%) developed detectable KRAS codon 12/13 mutations in serum during therapy, 3 of whom developed multiple different KRAS mutations (2 in one patient and 4 in two others); none developed BRAF mutations. The authors suggested that emergence of KRAS mutations is a mediator of acquired resistance to EGFR blockade and can be detected noninvasively.
quotes: We found that 9 out of 24 (38%) patients whose tumours were initially KRAS wild type developed detectable mutations in KRAS in their sera, three of which developed multiple different KRAS mutations.

Of the 24 patients who did not have KRAS mutations at baseline, nine (38%) were found to develop KRAS mutations during the course of therapy (Supplementary Table 2) while none developed BRAF mutations.
These results suggest that the emergence of KRAS mutations is a mediator of acquired resistance to EGFR blockade and that these mutations can be detected in a non-invasive manner.

findings.statement: Diaz et al. (2012) found that in KRAS-wildtype metastatic colorectal cancer patients treated with panitumumab, the appearance of circulating KRAS mutations was very consistent, generally occurring 5 to 6 months after treatment initiation (23 +/- 5 weeks), and mutant KRAS was detected before radiographic progression in 3 of 9 cases with an average lead time of 21 weeks. Circulating tumor DNA levels generally paralleled CEA. Progression-free and overall survival did not differ significantly between those who did and did not develop secondary KRAS mutations.
quotes: The appearance of these mutations was very consistent, generally occurring between 5 and 6 months following treatment.

Circulating mutant KRAS templates were identified prior to radiographic evidence of disease progression in three of the nine cases (Patients #1, 10 and 24). The lead time (i.e., the interval between detectable ctDNA and radiographic evidence of disease progression) averaged 21 weeks
of patients was not significantly different whether they developed secondary KRAS mutations or not

findings.statement: Using mathematical modeling of serial circulating tumor DNA data, Diaz et al. (2012) concluded that KRAS mutations conferring resistance to panitumumab were present in expanded subclones before therapy began, and estimated that about 42 nucleotides (in perhaps about 10 genes) could confer resistance, with each large metastatic lesion expected to harbor hundreds to thousands of resistant cells before treatment. They suggested that resistance is a 'fait accompli' and that combination therapies targeting at least two pathways would be required for longer remissions.
quotes: Mathematical modelling indicated that the mutations were present in expanded subclones before the initiation of panitumumab treatment.
Each relatively large metastatic lesion is expected to contain a subclone containing hundreds or thousands of cells with one of ~42 mutations conferring resistance to the antibody.
To make these remissions last longer than five to six months, combination therapies targeting at least two different pathways will be required.

findings.statement: Diaz et al. (2012) found that in 3 of 4 metastatic colorectal cancer patients with KRAS-mutant archival tumors, the identical KRAS mutation was detectable in pretreatment serum, whereas no KRAS mutations were detected in pretreatment serum of patients with KRAS-wildtype tumors, supporting circulating tumor DNA as a 'liquid biopsy.'
quotes: Of the four cases whose archival tumors harbored KRAS mutations, three had detectable levels of mutant KRAS in the serum prior to treatment with panitumumab (Supplementary Table 2).
No mutations in KRAS were detected in the pre-treatment serum DNA from patients whose archival tumor tissue was WT for KRAS (Supplementary Table 2).

relevance_reason: Functional and therapeutic study of BRAF V600E-mutant colon cancer that explains why these tumors resist vemurafenib and proposes combining BRAF and EGFR inhibitors.

findings.statement: Prahallad et al. (2012) found that colon cancers with the BRAF V600E mutation respond poorly to the BRAF inhibitor PLX4032 (vemurafenib). In an RNA-interference screen of kinases in human cells, blocking EGFR was strongly synergistic with BRAF V600E inhibition. In multiple BRAF V600E-mutant colon cancers, inhibiting EGFR with cetuximab, gefitinib, or erlotinib was strongly synergistic with BRAF V600E inhibition both in vitro and in vivo. The authors suggested that BRAF V600E-mutant colon cancers, about 8 to 10% of all colon cancers, might benefit from combined BRAF and EGFR inhibitors.
quotes: We find in multiple BRAF(V600E) mutant colon cancers that inhibition of EGFR by the antibody drug cetuximab or the small-molecule drugs gefitinib or erlotinib is strongly synergistic with BRAF(V600E) inhibition, both in vitro and in vivo.

Our data suggest that BRAF(V600E) mutant colon cancers (approximately 8-10% of all colon cancers), for which there are currently no targeted treatment options available, might benefit from combination therapy consisting of BRAF and EGFR inhibitors.
colon cancer patients harbouring the same BRAF(V600E) oncogenic lesion have poor prognosis and show only a very limited response to this drug

findings.statement: Prahallad et al. (2012) found that inhibiting BRAF V600E in colon cancer cells caused rapid feedback activation of EGFR, which allowed the cells to keep proliferating despite the BRAF inhibition. Melanoma cells express low levels of EGFR and were not subject to this feedback. Ectopic expression of EGFR in melanoma cells was sufficient to cause resistance to PLX4032.
quotes: Mechanistically, we find that BRAF(V600E) inhibition causes a rapid feedback activation of EGFR, which supports continued proliferation in the presence of BRAF(V600E) inhibition.
Melanoma cells express low levels of EGFR and are therefore not subject to this feedback activation.
we find that ectopic expression of EGFR in melanoma cells is sufficient to cause resistance to PLX4032

relevance_reason: Reports an acquired somatic EGFR ectodomain mutation (S492R) conferring cetuximab resistance in colorectal cancer patients, relevant to the molecular genetics/management sections of the CRC entry.

findings.statement: Montagut et al. (2012) identified an acquired somatic mutation in the EGFR ectodomain, S492R, in 2 of 10 colorectal cancer patients with disease progression after cetuximab treatment. The mutation prevented cetuximab binding and conferred resistance to cetuximab, whereas cells with the mutation retained binding to and were growth inhibited by panitumumab.
quotes: We describe an acquired EGFR ectodomain mutation (S492R) that prevents cetuximab binding and confers resistance to cetuximab.
Cells with this mutation, however, retain binding to and are growth inhibited by panitumumab.
Two of ten subjects studied here with disease progression after cetuximab treatment acquired this mutation.

findings.statement: Montagut et al. (2012) reported that a colorectal cancer patient with cetuximab resistance whose tumor harbored the acquired EGFR S492R mutation responded to treatment with panitumumab.
quotes: A subject with cetuximab resistance harboring the S492R mutation responded to treatment with panitumumab.

relevance_reason: The paper identifies a mutant HSP110 (HSPH1) in colorectal cancer with microsatellite instability and links its expression to prognosis and response to chemotherapy. This adds somatic and prognostic evidence for the colorectal cancer entry.

findings.statement: Dorard et al. (2011) identified a mutant of HSP110, HSP110-delta-E9, in colorectal cancers with microsatellite instability (MSI CRC). The mutant was generated from an aberrantly spliced mRNA and lacked the HSP110 substrate-binding domain. It was expressed at variable levels in almost all MSI CRC cell lines and primary tumors tested.
quotes: We identified a mutant of HSP110 (HSP110ΔE9) in colorectal cancer showing microsatellite instability (MSI CRC), generated from an aberrantly spliced mRNA and lacking the HSP110 substrate-binding domain.
This mutant was expressed at variable levels in almost all MSI CRC cell lines and primary tumors tested.

findings.statement: Dorard et al. (2011) found that HSP110-delta-E9 disrupted the normal cellular localization of HSP110 and its interaction with other HSPs. In a dominant-negative manner, it abolished the chaperone activity and antiapoptotic function of HSP110. Overexpression of HSP110-delta-E9 made cells more sensitive to oxaliplatin and 5-fluorouracil.
quotes: HSP110ΔE9 impaired both the normal cellular localization of HSP110 and its interaction with other HSPs, thus abrogating the chaperone activity and antiapoptotic function of HSP110 in a dominant-negative manner.
HSP110ΔE9 overexpression caused the sensitization of cells to anticancer agents such as oxaliplatin and 5-fluorouracil

findings.statement: Dorard et al. (2011) found that survival and response to chemotherapy in patients with MSI colorectal cancer were associated with the level of HSP110-delta-E9 expression in the tumor. They suggested that HSP110 may be a major determinant of both prognosis and treatment response in colorectal cancer.
quotes: The survival and response to chemotherapy of subjects with MSI CRCs was associated with the tumor expression level of HSP110ΔE9.
HSP110 may thus constitute a major determinant for both prognosis and treatment response in CRC.

relevance_reason: The study whole-genome sequenced colorectal adenocarcinomas and found a recurrent somatic VTI1A-TCF7L2 fusion, with functional data. This is somatic genetic evidence that bears on the colorectal cancer entry.

findings.statement: Bass et al. (2011) performed whole-genome sequencing on 9 primary colorectal adenocarcinomas and matched adjacent non-tumor tissue, at average coverages of 30.7x and 31.9x. The mutation rate was about 5.9 per Mb (range, 4.0-9.8), with a strong predilection for C-to-T transitions at CpG sites. KRAS, APC, and TP53 were mutated in 5, 7, and 6 tumors, respectively, and scored as significantly recurrent.
quotes: Using all candidate mutations, we calculated an overall mutation rate of ~5.9 per Mb with a range of 4.0–9.8 mutations per Mb relative to a haploid genome (Table 1).
Indeed, we noted mutations in KRAS, APC and TP53 in five, seven and six individuals’ tumors, respectively (Supplementary Table 2).

findings.statement: Bass et al. (2011) found an average of 75 somatic rearrangements per tumor (range, 5-182) across 9 colorectal cancer genomes. Three tumors showed clustered networks of balanced interchromosomal translocations between pairs of chromosomes, including chromosomes 8 and 20 in one tumor and chromosomes 5 and 11 in another. The authors described these as a variant of the chromothripsis pattern. They also found small deletions that removed the first exon of EGFR and the 3-prime section of PTEN.
quotes: we identified 675 candidate somatic rearrangements across the nine tumors (mean, 75; range 5–182; Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 4)
We saw networks of fusions between chromosomes 8 and 20 in CRC-4 and chromosomes 5 and 11 in CRC-6 (Fig. 2).
including a deletion that removed the first exon of EGFR in CRC-9 and a deletion removing the 3′ section of PTEN in CRC-8

findings.statement: Bass et al. (2011) identified 11 rearrangements across 9 colorectal cancer genomes that were predicted to produce in-frame fusions. One of these joined the first 3 exons of VTI1A to exon 4 of the adjacent TCF7L2 gene on chromosome 10, caused by an approximately 540-kb deletion. Screening cDNA from 97 primary colorectal cancers found in-frame VTI1A-TCF7L2 fusions in 3 tumors (3%). The fusion protein lacks the N-terminal beta-catenin-binding domain of TCF4. All 3 fusion-positive tumors also carried APC alterations.
quotes: We found in-frame VTI1A-TCF7L2 fusions in two additional cases and three of 97 total primary colorectal carcinomas (including the CRC-9 index case) (Supplementary Fig. 2).
fusing the first three exons of VTI1A, which encodes a v-SNARE protein mediating fusion of intracellular vesicles within the Golgi complex, to the fourth exon of the adjacent gene, TCF7L2 (Fig. 3a–c)
However, the three tumors harboring the fusion protein also carry mutations in APC, whose product suppresses β-catenin.

variants.as_reported: VTI1A exon 3 to TCF7L2 exon 4 fusion

findings.statement: Bass et al. (2011) found a point mutation in TCF7L2 in one colorectal tumor that affected the splice site at the 3-prime end of exon 10, the exon encoding the HMG-box DNA-binding domain. The authors considered this mutation likely deleterious.
quotes: We additionally found a point mutation in CRC-5 affecting the splice-site at the 3′ end of exon 10, which is the exon encoding the HMG-box DNA binding domain, that would likely be a deleterious mutation.

variants.as_reported: splice-site mutation at 3' end of exon 10

findings.statement: Bass et al. (2011) showed that the colorectal cancer cell line NCI-H508 carries a deletion producing an in-frame fusion of VTI1A exon 2 to TCF7L2 exon 5. Knocking down the fusion transcript with shRNA sharply reduced anchorage-independent growth of NCI-H508 cells but not of the fusion-negative DLD-1 cells. NCI-H508 also depended on beta-catenin. The authors suggested that VTI1A-TCF7L2 is expressed in the setting of activated beta-catenin.
quotes: Two vectors that reduced the expression of the fusion mRNA by >70% as gauged by quantitative RT-PCR caused a dramatic reduction in the anchorage-independent growth of cells from NCI-H508 but not DLD-1, a colorectal cancer cell line that does not harbor the fusion gene (Fig. 3d,e).

These results suggest that VTI1A-TCF7L2 is expressed in the setting of activated β-catenin and that NCI-H508 is dependent on both the fusion gene and β-catenin despite the deletion of the VTI1A-TCF7L2 β-catenin binding domain.

relevance_reason: Case-control association study showing that germline heterozygosity for the PKHD1 T36M mutation is protective against colorectal cancer.

findings.statement: Ward et al. (2011) screened 2 European-origin cohorts with sporadic colorectal adenocarcinoma and 2 age- and sex-matched control cohorts for the most common European PKHD1 mutation, T36M (107C-T). In the first study, they found 6 T36M heterozygotes among 1,601 controls (0.37%) and none among 1,842 colorectal cancer patients (p = 0.01). In the second study, they found 9 among 2,002 controls (0.45%) and 1 among 1,925 cancer patients (0.05%) (p = 0.022). Combined, T36M was found in 15 of 3,603 controls (0.42%) and 1 of 3,767 colorectal cancer patients (0.027%) (p = 0.0002; odds ratio 0.072). The authors concluded that heterozygous PKHD1 mutations are not a risk factor for colorectal cancer and are protective.
quotes: Six T36M heterozygotes were found in the control sample (0.37%), and none (0.0%) in the colorectal cancer sample (p=0.01 Fisher's exact test).
In this second study, we found nine T36M heterozygotes in the control sample (0.45%, n=2002 subjects) and one in the colorectal cancer sample (0.05%, n=1925 subjects) (p=0.022).

Screening for the most common PKHD1 mutation, T36M, we detected 15:3,603 (0.42%) controls versus 1:3,767 (0.027%) colorectal cancer individuals, indicating that heterozygous PKHD1 mutations are not a risk factor and are protective (p=0.0002).

findings.statement: Ward et al. (2011) hypothesized that reduced fibrocystin activity could cause mitotic instability and centrosome amplification, so that premalignant cells have too much genomic instability to form aggressive tumors, which would explain the protective effect of the PKHD1 T36M mutation against colorectal carcinoma.
quotes: One possible hypothesis to explain the findings is that reduction of fibrocystin activity might result in enhanced mitotic instability which paradoxically inhibits carcinogenesis.

It may be that germline mutations in PKHD1 act similarly, inducing susceptibility to centrosomal amplification in certain contexts, so that pre-malignant cells have too much genomic instability to form aggressive tumors

findings.statement: Ward et al. (2011) found that T36M made up 13.1% of PKHD1 mutations in a European ARPKD cohort. Using the T36M frequency in controls, they estimated the carrier frequency of all PKHD1 mutations in the European population at 3.2% (1 in 31), higher than the previous estimate of 1 in 70.
quotes: First, we assayed a European cohort of ARPKD patients and found T36M was responsible for 13.1% of mutations.
to project a 3.2% (7.6 × 0.42), 1:31 carrier frequency for PKHD1 in the European population (3.2%, 95% CI:1.7–5.9%).

relevance_reason: Reports a large Utah kindred with excess colorectal cancer and adenomas that linked to a susceptibility locus on 13q22.1-q31.3. This is mapping evidence for a CRC susceptibility locus, but no causal gene was found.

findings.statement: Neklason et al. (2010) described a large Utah kindred (K5275), identified through the Utah Population Database, with a statistical excess of colorectal cancer (familial standardized incidence ratio 12.4). The family showed no clinical or molecular features of known hereditary colon cancer syndromes. In the 4 generations studied, the average age at colon cancer diagnosis was 46 years and the average age at detection of the first adenoma was 49.5 years. Of 32 kindred members who had colonoscopy, 3 had CRC, 9 had adenomatous polyps, and 22 had no adenomas. No one had more than 5 adenomas. No affected member had advanced adenomas, but 2 of the 3 cancers (diagnosed at ages 42 and 35) were metastatic at diagnosis, which the authors took as a subtle suggestion that adenomas may advance rapidly to metastasis.
quotes: The average age of colon cancer in this branch was 46 and the average age when the first adenoma was detected was 49.5.
Three family members had CRC, 9 family members and two spouses had adenomatous polyps, and 22 family members had no adenomatous polyps.
We note that no affected family members had advanced adenomas (≥10 mm or advanced histology), however two of the three colon cancers were metastatic at diagnosis (age 42 and 35)

findings.statement: In the K5275 kindred, Neklason et al. (2010) excluded Lynch syndrome because 2 colorectal cancers were microsatellite stable, and they found no evidence of polyposis syndromes. LOD scores were negative near the known familial colon cancer genes APC, MYH, CTNNB1, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, STK11, PTEN, and BMPR1A. One marker near SMAD4 was positive, but the other markers near SMAD4 gave negative LOD scores.
quotes: Two CRC cases (II-6 and III-13) showed microsatellite stability, indicating that this family does not have Lynch Syndrome.
LOD scores were negative in regions surrounding genes known to cause familial colon cancer (APC, MYH, CTNNB1, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, STK11, PTEN, BMPR1A).

findings.statement: Neklason et al. (2010) performed genomewide STR and SNP linkage scans of kindred K5275 and identified a single major locus on chromosome 13q that segregated with adenomatous polyps and colon cancer. Under an autosomal dominant model, the maximum 2-point LOD score was 2.43 at D13S251. Nonparametric analysis gave a maximum NPL score of 24.12 (LOD 2.99, p = 0.001) at D13S251. The nonrecombinant region spanned rs1870836 (13q22.2) to D13S265 (13q31.3), about 21 Mb containing 27 RefSeq genes.
quotes: The linkage analysis, specifying an autosomal dominant model, generated a maximum 2-point LOD score of 2.43 for the STR marker D13S251 on chromosome 13.
yielded a maximum nonparametric linkage (NPL) score of 24.12 (LOD score of 2.99 and p=0.001) at D13S251 when individuals II-4, III-4, and III-5 were coded as unknown
When this individual is excluded, the nonrecombinant region spans rs1870836 (75,454,410 Mbp; 13q22.2) to D13S265 (89,171,101 Mbp; 13q31.3).

findings.statement: Neklason et al. (2010) sequenced 8 candidate cancer-related genes in the 13q linked region: KLF5, KLF12, LMO7, RNF219, SPRY2, GPC5, MYCBP2, and POU4F1. They found no unambiguously deleterious mutation. They did find polymorphisms that segregated with the phenotype, including SNPs in SPRY2, RNF219, LMO7, and KLF12 and a novel SNP in the POU4F1 promoter. Whether these SNPs were causative or in disequilibrium with the causal change could not be determined.
quotes: No unambiguously deleterious mutations have been identified in these genes; however SNPs segregating with the colon cancer and polyp phenotype were identified (Table 2).
There is no evidence to indicate if these are in disequilibrium with the responsible change or if they are causative.

findings.statement: Neklason et al. (2010) performed CGH on a metastatic colon cancer from an obligate carrier of the 13q haplotype (diagnosed at age 42). It showed duplication of most of 13q, plus losses typical of sporadic CRC (APC, TP53, DCC, SMAD4). In STR peak-ratio analysis, all 3 family cancers showed a copy number gain at 1 of 3 13q markers, whereas 2 adenomas showed no change. Because 13q is gained in 30 to 50% of CRCs and correlates with metastasis, the authors suggested that the locus may harbor a gain-of-function cancer progression gene.
quotes: CGH analysis revealed duplication of the majority of chromosome 13q (Figure S1, panel A)
The adenomas showed no change, however all three cancers showed a copy number increase at one of three markers.
There is a reasonable chance that a clear deleterious mutation will not be identified because evidence from sporadic CRCs suggests that there is a gain of function (oncogene) at 13q.

relevance_reason: A review of microsatellite instability in colorectal cancer covering how often it occurs, its molecular causes (germline mismatch repair mutations, MLH1 hypermethylation, BRAF V600E), clinical and pathological features, prognosis and response to chemotherapy. It reports no new patients, but it summarizes evidence relevant to the CRC entry.

findings.statement: Vilar and Gruber (2010) reviewed microsatellite instability (MSI) in colorectal cancer, noting that approximately 15% of colorectal cancers display MSI. This is due either to epigenetic silencing of MLH1 or to a germline mutation in one of the mismatch repair genes MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2. They stated that most MSI colorectal cancers are sporadic and caused by MLH1 promoter hypermethylation, whereas 2 to 3% of all colorectal cancers are caused by germline mismatch repair gene mutations (Lynch syndrome).
quotes: Approximately 15% of colorectal cancers (CRC) display MSI owing either to epigenetic silencing of MLH1 or a germline mutation in one of the mismatch repair genes MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2.
Approximately 15% of colorectal cancers (CRC) display microsatellite instability (MSI), and most are nonfamilial (sporadic) and caused by hypermethylation of the MLH1 promoter
2–3% of all CRCs are caused by germline mutations in one of the mismatch repair genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 and PMS2)

findings.statement: Vilar and Gruber (2010) noted that population-based studies have reported MSI in 8 to 20% of colorectal cancers. MSI was more common in stage II (about 20%) than in stage III (about 12%) or stage IV (about 4%) tumors. They also noted that 2 small retrospective studies suggested a higher frequency of MSI tumors in African American (20-45%) and Egyptian (37%) populations.
quotes: Several population-based studies have reported that the prevalence of MSI in CRC ranges from 8% to 20%, although these values might differ according to stage distribution.
MSI is more common among stage II (~20%) than stage III (~12%) CRC, and is even less frequent among stage IV CRC (~4%).
two small retrospective studies suggest that MSI tumors are more frequent in African American (20–45%) and Egyptian (37%) populations.

findings.statement: Vilar and Gruber (2010) summarized the clinical and pathological profile of MSI colorectal cancers. These tumors tend to be right-sided and diagnosed at lower pathological stages, with high histological grade, mucinous features, prominent tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, absence of dirty necrosis, and a Crohn-like host response. Sporadic MSI cases are generally diagnosed after age 70 years, whereas familial cases are diagnosed before age 50 years.
quotes: CRC displaying MSI tend to be right-sided and diagnosed at lower pathological stages compared with MSS cancers.
sporadic MSI cases are generally diagnosed in older patients (> 70 years of age), and familial cases are younger (< 50 years of age) and show a U-shaped age distribution.

Under the microscope CRC generally have high histological grades, mucinous phenotypes with prominent numbers of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, a lack of dirty necrosis and a Crohn-like host response.

findings.statement: Vilar and Gruber (2010) noted that BRAF mutations, mostly V600E in exon 15, are present in 10% of colorectal cancers and do not occur together with KRAS mutations. BRAF mutations are more frequent in sporadic MSI tumors with MLH1 hypermethylation than in hereditary (Lynch syndrome) cases. KRAS mutations, present in about 40% of primary colorectal tumors, are more frequent in microsatellite-stable tumors (those with chromosomal instability) than in MSI tumors.
quotes: BRAF mutations are present in 10% of CRC and are mutually exclusive with KRAS mutations. Most of these mutations are located in a hotspot located in exon 15 that leads to a V600E single-amino-acid substitution.
Strikingly, BRAF mutations in colorectal tumors are more frequent in sporadic MSI tumors caused by hypermethylation of MLH1 than in the hereditary cases.
Indeed, KRAS mutations are present in approximately 40% of colorectal primary tumors.

findings.statement: Vilar and Gruber (2010) noted that PI3K pathway genes are altered in about 40% of colorectal tumors. PIK3CA mutation rates were reported at 10 to 30%, and other genes in the pathway (PDK1, AKT2, PAK4, IRS2, INSRR, ERBB4, PTEN) were also mutated. PTEN was both mutated and frequently epigenetically silenced in MSI tumors.
quotes: Subsequent studies found lower mutation rates (10–20%) in different populations, although most of these studies only examined mutational hotspots in exons 9 and 20.
PTEN, which is the only tumor suppressor in this pathway, is not only mutated, but also epigenetically silenced with high frequency in MSI tumors.

findings.statement: Vilar and Gruber (2010) described how MSI is detected using the Bethesda panel of 5 microsatellite markers (BAT25, BAT26, D5S346, D2S123, D17S250). Tumors are classified as MSI-high (2 or more unstable loci), MSI-low, or microsatellite stable. Immunohistochemistry for MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2 indicates which gene is most likely inactivated. Loss of MLH1 is typically accompanied by loss of PMS2, and MLH1 promoter methylation is typically accompanied by somatic BRAF V600E.
quotes: This reference panel, known as the Bethesda panel, included five microsatellite loci—two mononucleotides (BAT25 and BAT26) and three dinucleotides (D5S346, D2S123 and D17S250).

Lack of expression of one or more of these proteins is diagnostic of deficient MMR, and determines which gene is most likely to harbor a germline mutation or to have been inactivated by another mechanism.
Methylation of the MLH1 promoter is typically accompanied by BRAF V600E somatic mutations.

findings.statement: Vilar and Gruber (2010) reviewed a meta-analysis of 32 studies with 7,642 cases, 1,277 of them MSI. It confirmed that MSI colorectal cancers have a better prognosis and spread less often to lymph nodes and distant sites than microsatellite-stable cancers. Data from 6 randomized trials (Sargent et al.) suggested that 5-FU-based adjuvant chemotherapy gives no benefit, and might even be harmful, in stage II MSI tumors. Evidence for a benefit from irinotecan in MSI tumors remained preliminary and conflicting.
quotes: Individual clinical data from a total of 32 studies were considered in a meta-analysis that included 7,642 cases, where 1,277 of these displayed MSI. The meta-analysis confirmed the prognostic advantage of MSI.
Sargent et al. concluded that 5-FU has no advantage over no 5-FU and might even be harmful for stage II cases displaying MSI

findings.statement: Vilar and Gruber (2010) noted that MSI colorectal cancers usually have a stable karyotype, unlike chromosomally unstable tumors. In mismatch repair-deficient tumors, frameshift mutations occur in coding microsatellites of more than 30 genes, including TGFBR2, IGF2R, BAX, MSH3, MSH6, MRE11A, and RAD50. MRE11A mutations are found in 70 to 85% of MSI tumors and may increase sensitivity to irinotecan.
quotes: By contrast, MSI CRCs tend to show a stable karyotype (CIN negative), and genetic instability in this subtype of CRC primarily reflects variation in microsatellite tracts owing to a defective MMR system (Figure 4b).
Mutations in this gene are detected in 70–85% of MSI tumors, making MSI an imperfect surrogate marker for increased sensitivity to irinotecan.

relevance_reason: Functional study of colon cells showing that genes synergistically regulated by p53 loss and Ras activation ('cooperation response genes') are critical to tumor formation; relevant to colorectal cancer pathogenesis.

findings.statement: McMurray et al. (2008) showed that a large proportion of genes controlled synergistically by loss-of-function p53 and Ras activation ('cooperation response genes') were critical to the malignant state of murine and human colon cells. In gene perturbation experiments, 14 of 24 cooperation response genes contributed to tumor formation, compared with only 1 of 14 perturbations of non-synergistically responding genes. The authors suggested that synergistic control of gene expression by oncogenic mutations is an underlying key to malignancy and provides a rationale for identifying intervention targets.
quotes: Here we show that a large proportion of genes controlled synergistically by loss-of-function p53 and Ras activation are critical to the malignant state of murine and human colon cells.

Notably, 14 out of 24 'cooperation response genes' were found to contribute to tumour formation in gene perturbation experiments. In contrast, only 1 in 14 perturbations of the genes responding in a non-synergistic manner had a similar effect.

relevance_reason: The paper reports somatic MYH11 mutations in colorectal cancers, mostly microsatellite-unstable tumours, and functional studies showing these mutations produce unregulated myosin. This adds evidence about the somatic genetics of CRC.

findings.statement: Alhopuro et al. (2008) screened patients with colorectal cancer, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, and juvenile polyposis for MYH11 mutations. They found somatic protein-elongating frameshift mutations in MYH11 in 55% of colorectal cancers with microsatellite instability. They also found 2 somatic missense mutations, R501L and K1044N, in one microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer.
quotes: We found somatic protein-elongating frameshift mutations in 55% of CRCs displaying microsatellite instability and in the germ-line of one individual with PJS.
Additionally, two somatic missense mutations were found in one microsatellite stable CRC.

findings.statement: Alhopuro et al. (2008) tested the R501L and K1044N missense mutations and the frameshift mutations in MYH11. All of them produced unregulated myosin molecules with constitutive motor activity, similar to the mutant myosin that causes the zebrafish meltdown phenotype. The authors suggested that unregulated MYH11 may affect cellular energy balance or disturb cell lineage decisions in tumor progenitor cells.
quotes: These two missense mutations, R501L and K1044N, and the frameshift mutations were functionally evaluated. All mutations resulted in unregulated molecules displaying constitutive motor activity, similar to the mutant myosin underlying mlt.
Unregulated MYH11 may affect the cellular energy balance or disturb cell lineage decisions in tumor progenitor cells.

relevance_reason: Genome-wide linkage scan of familial colorectal neoplasia kindreds that identified susceptibility loci (1p31.1, 15q14-q22, 17p13.3, 21, BRCA2 region).

findings.statement: Daley et al. (2008) performed a genome-wide linkage scan of 194 kindreds with familial colorectal neoplasia from the colon neoplasia sibling study. Families were classified into 5 phenotypic subgroups (severe histopathology, oligopolyposis, young, colon/breast, and multiple cancer), and affected, unaffected, and discordant sib pairs were analyzed. Sib-pair linkage statistics and Haseman-Elston regression identified 19 linkage peaks, with notable results for chromosomes 1p31.1, 15q14-q22, 17p13.3, and 21.
quotes: the colon neoplasia sibling study conducted a comprehensive, genome-wide linkage scan of 194 kindreds
Sib-pair linkage statistics and Haseman-Elston regression identified 19 linkage peaks, with interesting results for chromosomes 1p31.1, 15q14-q22, 17p13.3, and 21.

findings.statement: Daley et al. (2008) found strong evidence for linkage at marker D1S1665 on chromosome 1p31.1 in the multiple-cancer subgroup of familial colorectal neoplasia families (p = 0.00007).
quotes: At marker D1S1665 (1p31.1), there was strong evidence for linkage in the multiple-cancer subgroup (p = 0.00007).

findings.statement: Daley et al. (2008) identified a linkage peak on chromosome 15q14-q22 in the full sample (p = 0.018) and in the oligopolyposis (p = 0.003) and young-onset (p = 0.0009) subgroups. This region includes the HMPS/CRAC1 locus associated with hereditary mixed polyposis syndrome in Ashkenazi families, and the authors provided evidence linking this region in families of European descent with oligopolyposis and/or young age at onset (51 years or younger).
quotes: For chromosome 15q14-q22, a linkage peak was identified in the full-sample (p = 0.018), oligopolyposis (p = 0.003), and young (p = 0.0009) phenotypes.
This region includes the HMPS/CRAC1 locus associated with hereditary mixed polyposis syndrome (HMPS) in families of Ashkenazi descent.
We provide compelling evidence linking this region in families of European descent with oligopolyposis and/or young age at onset (<or=51) phenotypes.

findings.statement: In the colon/breast cancer subgroup, Daley et al. (2008) found linkage to BRCA2 and identified a second locus near D21S1437 on chromosome 21 segregating with, but distinct from, BRCA2. Linkage to 17p13.3 at marker D17S1308 in the breast/colon subgroup identified HIC1 as a candidate gene.
quotes: We found linkage to BRCA2 in the colon/breast phenotypic subgroup and identified a second locus in the region of D21S1437 segregating with, but distinct from, BRCA2.
Linkage to 17p13.3 at marker D17S1308 in the breast/colon subgroup identified HIC1 as a candidate gene.

relevance_reason: Genome-wide sequencing of somatic mutations in colorectal (and breast) tumors that describes the somatic mutational landscape of colorectal cancer. Only the abstract was available.

findings.statement: Wood et al. (2007) sequenced exons representing 20,857 transcripts from 18,191 RefSeq genes in DNA from 11 colorectal and 11 breast tumors. They concluded that the genomic landscapes of these cancers consist of a handful of commonly mutated gene 'mountains' and a much larger number of gene 'hills' mutated at low frequency. They described statistical and bioinformatic tools that may help identify mutations with a role in tumorigenesis.
quotes: we isolated DNA from 11 breast and 11 colorectal tumors and determined the sequences of the genes in the Reference Sequence database in these samples

Based on analysis of exons representing 20,857 transcripts from 18,191 genes, we conclude that the genomic landscapes of breast and colorectal cancers are composed of a handful of commonly mutated gene "mountains" and a much larger number of gene "hills" that are mutated at low frequency

findings.statement: Wood et al. (2007) stated that their findings have implications for understanding the nature and heterogeneity of human cancers and for using personal genomics for tumor diagnosis and therapy.
quotes: These results have implications for understanding the nature and heterogeneity of human cancers and for using personal genomics for tumor diagnosis and therapy.

relevance_reason: A reanalysis of somatic mutation data from colorectal and breast cancers that questions whether the candidate cancer genes reported by Sjöblom et al. (2006) are really mutated more often than expected. A curator would cite it as a caveat in the somatic mutation discussion.

findings.statement: Rubin and Green (2007) reanalyzed the somatic mutation data of Sjöblom et al. (2006) from breast and colorectal cancers using what they considered more appropriate statistical methods and background mutation rate assumptions. They concluded that few if any of the newly reported candidate cancer genes had significantly elevated mutation rates.
quotes: Sjöblom et al. (Research Article, 13 October 2006, p. 268) reported many new genes with an apparent significant excess of mutations in breast and colorectal cancer.
Reanalysis of their data with more appropriate statistical methods and background mutation rate assumptions reveals that few if any of these genes have significantly elevated mutation rates.

relevance_reason: A statistical critique of a large-scale colorectal/breast cancer somatic mutation screen. It argues that few of the proposed cancer genes have significantly elevated mutation rates.

findings.statement: Getz et al. (2007) commented on the report by Sjoblom et al. of nearly 200 novel cancer genes said to have a 90% probability of involvement in colon or breast cancer. They raised two statistical concerns about that analysis and found that, once these were addressed, few genes with significantly elevated mutation rates remained. They concluded that more samples were needed to achieve sufficient power.
quotes: reported nearly 200 novel cancer genes said to have a 90% probability of being involved in colon or breast cancer. However, their analysis raises two statistical concerns.
When these concerns are addressed, few genes with significantly elevated mutation rates remain.
more samples are needed to achieve sufficient power.

relevance_reason: This comment critiques the statistics Sjöblom et al. used to find colorectal and breast cancer genes. It argues that redoing the analysis correctly leaves far fewer significantly mutated genes. OMIM cites such comments alongside the original study.

findings.statement: Forrest and Cavet (2007) commented on the cancer genome resequencing analysis of breast and colorectal cancers by Sjoblom et al. (2006). They stated that the earlier analysis used point probabilities when it should have used P values for the hypotheses being tested. When Forrest and Cavet (2007) reran the analysis method with exact P values, far fewer genes had mutation rates that reached statistical significance.
quotes: Their analysis used point probabilities when it should have used P values for the hypotheses they intended to test.
Reimplementing their analysis method with exact P values results in far fewer genes with mutation rates that achieve statistical significance.

relevance_reason: Large-scale somatic mutation sequencing of colorectal (and breast) cancers that identified candidate cancer genes mutated at significant frequency. It adds somatic mutation context but names no specific gene or variant in the abstract.

findings.statement: Sjöblom et al. (2006) sequenced 13,023 well-annotated human protein-coding genes in 11 breast and 11 colorectal cancers. They found that individual tumors accumulated an average of about 90 mutant genes, but only a subset of these contributed to the neoplastic process. Using stringent criteria, they identified 189 genes (an average of 11 per tumor) that were mutated at significant frequency. Most of these genes were not previously known to be genetically altered in tumors and were predicted to affect functions including transcription, adhesion, and invasion.
quotes: Analysis of 13,023 genes in 11 breast and 11 colorectal cancers revealed that individual tumors accumulate an average of approximately 90 mutant genes but that only a subset of these contribute to the neoplastic process.
Using stringent criteria to delineate this subset, we identified 189 genes (average of 11 per tumor) that were mutated at significant frequency.
The vast majority of these genes were not known to be genetically altered in tumors and are predicted to affect a wide range of cellular functions, including transcription, adhesion, and invasion.

relevance_reason: Case-control association study linking TLR2 GT microsatellite and TLR4 Asp299Gly polymorphisms with sporadic colorectal cancer susceptibility in Croatians.

findings.statement: Boraska Jelavić et al. (2006) genotyped the TLR2 GT microsatellite polymorphism and the TLR2 Arg753Gln polymorphism in 89 Croatian patients with sporadic colorectal cancer and 88 age- and sex-matched controls. In patients, TLR2 GT microsatellite alleles with 20 and 21 GT repeats were less frequent (p = 0.0044 and p = 0.001, respectively) and the allele with 31 GT repeats was more frequent (p = 0.0147). The authors reported an association of the TLR2 GT microsatellite polymorphism with sporadic colorectal cancer.
quotes: We assessed genotype and allele frequencies of TLR2 GT microsatelite polymorphism, TLR2 Arg753Gln, TLR4 Asp299Gly and TLR4 Thr399Ile polymorphisms in 89 colorectal cancer patients and 88 age- and sex-matched controls.

The frequency of TLR2 GT microsatelite alleles with 20 and 21 GT repeats was decreased (p = 0.0044 and p = 0.001, respectively), while the frequency of the allele with 31 GT repeats was increased (p = 0.0147) in patients.
In conclusion, we report an association of microsatelite GT polymorphisms of TLR2 gene and Asp299Gly polymorphism of the TLR4 gene with sporadic colorectal cancer among Croatians.

findings.statement: In the same case-control study of 89 Croatian sporadic colorectal cancer patients and 88 matched controls, Boraska Jelavić et al. (2006) found that the mutant Asp299Gly allele of TLR4 was slightly more frequent in patients (p = 0.0269), and reported an association of this polymorphism with sporadic colorectal cancer; TLR4 Thr399Ile was also genotyped.
quotes: The mutant allele Asp299Gly of TLR4 gene was slightly more frequent in colorectal cancer patients (p = 0.0269).
In conclusion, we report an association of microsatelite GT polymorphisms of TLR2 gene and Asp299Gly polymorphism of the TLR4 gene with sporadic colorectal cancer among Croatians.

relevance_reason: Studies how mitochondrial DNA mutations spread in normal human colon by crypt fission; speculative implications for colorectal neoplasm growth; no CRC patients or variants.

findings.statement: Greaves et al. (2006) showed that nononcogenic mitochondrial DNA mutations established in colonic crypt stem cells spread through the normal human colon by crypt fission: mutated cytochrome c oxidase-deficient crypts undergoing fission and neighboring mutated crypts shared the same mitochondrial genotype, which differed from adjacent cytochrome c oxidase-positive crypts; mutated crypts were clustered throughout the colon, and patches of cytochrome c oxidase-deficient crypts increased in size with age. The authors suggested this may have implications for the growth and spread of colorectal neoplasms.
quotes: mutated crypts in the process of fission share the same mutated mitochondrial genotype not present in neighboring cytochrome c oxidase-positive crypts
patches of cytochrome c oxidase-deficient crypts increase in size with age

We thus demonstrate definitively that crypt fission is the mechanism by which mutations spread in the normal human colon. This has important implications for the biology of the normal adult human colon and possibly for the growth and spread of colorectal neoplasms.

relevance_reason: Somatic mutation screen of 340 serine/threonine kinases in colorectal cancers. It found mutations in 8 genes, including 3 members of the PI3K pathway. Only the abstract is available, and it does not name the genes or the variants.

findings.statement: Parsons et al. (2005) analyzed human colorectal cancers for mutations in 340 serine/threonine kinases. They found mutations in 8 genes, including 3 members of the phosphatidylinositol-3-OH kinase (PI3K) pathway. The authors suggested that this mutational activation of a key cell-signaling pathway may provide new targets for therapeutic intervention.
quotes: We analysed human colorectal cancers for genetic mutations in 340 serine/threonine kinases and found mutations in eight genes, including in three members of the phosphatidylinositol-3-OH kinase (PI(3)K) pathway.
The discovery of this mutational activation of a key cell-signalling pathway may provide new targets for therapeutic intervention.

relevance_reason: Shows that loss of EphB expression marks progression from colorectal adenoma to carcinoma in human tumors and speeds up tumor formation in Apc(Min/+) mice. This is supporting evidence about how colorectal cancer develops.

findings.statement: Batlle et al. (2005) found that most human colorectal cancers lose EphB receptor expression at the adenoma-carcinoma transition, even though Wnt signaling remains constitutively active. EphB receptors are Tcf4 target genes. Loss of EphB expression correlated strongly with degree of malignancy. The authors concluded that loss of EphB expression is a critical step in colorectal cancer progression.
quotes: although Wnt signalling remains constitutively active, most human colorectal cancers lose expression of EphB at the adenoma-carcinoma transition
Loss of EphB expression strongly correlates with degree of malignancy.
Our data demonstrate that loss of EphB expression represents a critical step in colorectal cancer progression.

findings.statement: Batlle et al. (2005) found that reducing EphB activity in Apc(Min/+) mice accelerated tumorigenesis in the colon and rectum and led to the formation of aggressive adenocarcinomas.
quotes: reduction of EphB activity accelerates tumorigenesis in the colon and rectum of Apc(Min/+) mice, and results in the formation of aggressive adenocarcinomas

relevance_reason: Case-control screening of candidate genes (APC, AXIN1, CTNNB1, MLH1, MSH2) in patients with multiple colorectal adenomas. The authors say the results support a rare-variant model of multifactorial susceptibility to colorectal neoplasia.

findings.statement: Fearnhead et al. (2004) screened germline DNA from 124 patients with 3 to 100 histologically proven synchronous or metachronous colorectal adenomas. They tested all patients for the APC variants I1307K and E1317Q and looked for variants in AXIN1, CTNNB1, MLH1, and MSH2. Thirty of the 124 patients (24.9%) carried potentially pathogenic germline variants, compared with 55 (about 12%) of 483 random controls. The authors said this highly significant difference suggested that many rare variants together contribute to inherited susceptibility to colorectal adenomas.
quotes: Germ-line DNA was obtained from 124 patients with between 3 and 100 histologically proven synchronous or metachronous adenomatous polyps.

All patients were tested for the adenomatous polyposis coli variants I1307K and E1317Q, and variants were also sought in AXIN1 (axin), CTNNB1 (beta-catenin), and the mismatch repair genes hMLH1 and hMSH2.

Thirty of 124 (24.9%) patients carried potentially pathogenic germ-line variants as compared with 55 ( approximately 12%) of the controls. This overall difference is highly significant, suggesting that many rare variants collectively contribute to the inherited susceptibility to colorectal adenomas.

findings.statement: Fearnhead et al. (2004) noted that clear-cut Mendelian traits such as familial adenomatous polyposis and hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer account for less than 4% of colorectal cancers. They noted that another 20% are thought to arise in people with a significant inherited multifactorial susceptibility that is not obviously familial. Using multiple colorectal adenomas as a model, the authors tested the hypothesis that rare variants account for this multifactorial inheritance.
quotes: Clear-cut inherited Mendelian traits, such as familial adenomatous polyposis or hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer, account for <4% of colorectal cancers.
Another 20% of all colorectal cancers are thought to occur in individuals with a significant inherited multifactorial susceptibility to colorectal cancer that is not obviously familial.
The aim of this study was to explore this rare variant hypothesis for multifactorial inheritance by using multiple colorectal adenomas as the model.

findings.statement: Samuels et al. (2004) reported a high frequency of mutations in the PIK3CA gene in human cancers. Only the title was available, so the tumour types, the specific variants and the mutation frequencies are not known from this source.
quotes: High frequency of mutations of the PIK3CA gene in human cancers.

findings.statement: KLUGE (1964) reported on familial cancer of the colon.
