quotes: Mutational analysis of the tyrosine kinome in colorectal cancers.

relevance_reason: Pilot study linking loss of IGF2 imprinting in blood lymphocytes to family history of CRC, colorectal adenomas and CRC; proposes LOI as a marker of CRC risk.

findings.statement: Cui et al. (2003) noted that loss of imprinting (LOI) of the IGF2 gene, an epigenetic change, is found in the normal colonic mucosa of about 30% of colorectal cancer patients but in only 10% of healthy people.
quotes: Loss of imprinting (LOI), an epigenetic alteration affecting the insulin-like growth factor II gene (IGF2), is found in normal colonic mucosa of about 30% of colorectal cancer (CRC) patients, but it is found in only 10% of healthy individuals.

findings.statement: In a pilot study of 172 patients seen at a colonoscopy clinic, Cui et al. (2003) found that IGF2 LOI in lymphocytes was associated with CRC risk. The adjusted odds ratio was 5.15 for patients with a positive family history (95% CI, 1.70-16.96; P = 0.002), 3.46 for patients with adenomas (95% CI, 1.14-11.37; P = 0.026), and 21.7 for patients with CRC (95% CI, 3.48-153.6; P = 0.0005). The authors suggested that LOI, which can be assayed with a DNA-based blood test, may be a valuable predictive marker of an individual's CRC risk.
quotes: In a pilot study to investigate the utility of LOI as a marker of CRC risk, we evaluated 172 patients at a colonoscopy clinic.

The adjusted odds ratio for LOI in lymphocytes was 5.15 for patients with a positive family history [95% confidence interval (95% CI), 1.70 to 16.96; probability P = 0.002], 3.46 for patients with adenomas (95% CI, 1.14 to 11.37; P = 0.026), and 21.7 for patients with CRC (95% CI, 3.48 to 153.6; P = 0.0005).
LOI can be assayed with a DNA-based blood test, and it may be a valuable predictive marker of an individual's risk for CRC.

relevance_reason: Only the title ("Hereditary colorectal cancer") is available. It identifies a review on hereditary colorectal cancer that is relevant to this entry as context, but it contains no patient, variant or experimental data that could be quoted to support a finding.
Randomized chemoprevention trial showing low-dose aspirin reduces colorectal adenoma recurrence; relevant to clinical management/prevention of colorectal cancer.

findings.statement: Baron et al. (2003) performed a randomized, double-blind trial of aspirin as a chemopreventive agent in 1,121 patients with a recent history of histologically documented colorectal adenomas, assigned to placebo (372), 81 mg aspirin (377), or 325 mg aspirin (372) daily. Among the 1,084 patients (97%) with follow-up colonoscopy at least 1 year after randomization, the incidence of 1 or more adenomas was 47% with placebo, 38% with 81 mg aspirin, and 45% with 325 mg aspirin (global P = 0.04); relative risks of any adenoma were 0.81 (95% CI, 0.69-0.96) for 81 mg and 0.96 (95% CI, 0.81-1.13) for 325 mg.
quotes: We randomly assigned 1121 patients with a recent history of histologically documented adenomas to receive placebo (372 patients), 81 mg of aspirin (377 patients), or 325 mg of aspirin (372 patients) daily.

The incidence of one or more adenomas was 47 percent in the placebo group, 38 percent in the group given 81 mg of aspirin per day, and 45 percent in the group given 325 mg of aspirin per day (global P=0.04).

findings.statement: For advanced neoplasms (adenomas at least 1 cm or with tubulovillous or villous features, severe dysplasia, or invasive cancer), Baron et al. (2003) found relative risks of 0.59 (95% CI, 0.38-0.92) with 81 mg aspirin and 0.83 (95% CI, 0.55-1.23) with 325 mg aspirin compared with placebo. They concluded that low-dose aspirin has a moderate chemopreventive effect on adenomas in the large bowel.
quotes: For advanced neoplasms (adenomas measuring at least 1 cm in diameter or with tubulovillous or villous features, severe dysplasia, or invasive cancer), the respective relative risks were 0.59 (95 percent confidence interval, 0.38 to 0.92) and 0.83 (95 percent confidence interval, 0.55 to 1.23).
Low-dose aspirin has a moderate chemopreventive effect on adenomas in the large bowel.

relevance_reason: Randomized trial showing aspirin reduces recurrent colorectal adenomas in patients with previous colorectal cancer; relevant to clinical management/chemoprevention of CRC.

findings.statement: Sandler et al. (2003) conducted a randomized, double-blind trial in which 635 patients with previous colorectal cancer received either 325 mg of aspirin per day or placebo. Among the 517 patients with at least one colonoscopy (median 12.8 months after randomization), one or more adenomas were found in 17% of the aspirin group and 27% of the placebo group (P = 0.004). The adjusted relative risk of any recurrent adenoma with aspirin was 0.65 (95% CI, 0.46-0.91), and time to detection of a first adenoma was longer with aspirin (hazard ratio 0.64). The authors concluded that daily aspirin use is associated with a significant reduction in the incidence of colorectal adenomas in patients with previous colorectal cancer.
quotes: We randomly assigned 635 patients with previous colorectal cancer to receive either 325 mg of aspirin per day or placebo.
One or more adenomas were found in 17 percent of patients in the aspirin group and 27 percent of patients in the placebo group (P=0.004).
The adjusted relative risk of any recurrent adenoma in the aspirin group, as compared with the placebo group, was 0.65 (95 percent confidence interval, 0.46 to 0.91).
Daily use of aspirin is associated with a significant reduction in the incidence of colorectal adenomas in patients with previous colorectal cancer.

relevance_reason: Only the title is available. It shows the paper looked at BLM heterozygosity as a risk factor for colorectal cancer, which is relevant to colorectal cancer susceptibility. No results can be taken from the title alone.

findings.statement: Gruber et al. (2002) studied BLM heterozygosity in relation to the risk of colorectal cancer.
quotes: BLM heterozygosity and the risk of colorectal cancer.

relevance_reason: Reports somatic BRAF and KRAS mutations in colorectal cancers, finding that they are mutually exclusive and that BRAF mutation is linked to mismatch-repair status. This is relevant to the molecular genetics of CRC.

findings.statement: Rajagopalan et al. (2002) found that somatic BRAF mutations in colorectal cancers occurred only in tumors that did not carry KRAS mutations. They concluded that this gave genetic support for the idea that BRAF and KRAS mutations have equivalent effects in tumorigenesis.
quotes: Here we show that BRAF mutations in colorectal cancers occur only in tumours that do not carry mutations in a RAS gene known as KRAS
Our results not only provide genetic support for the idea that mutations in BRAF and KRAS exert equivalent effects in tumorigenesis

findings.statement: Rajagopalan et al. (2002) reported that BRAF mutation in colorectal tumors was linked to the tumors' mismatch-repair status. The authors stated that this emphasizes the role of repair processes in shaping the mutation spectra of human cancer.
quotes: BRAF mutation is linked to the proficiency of these tumours in repairing mismatched bases in DNA
also emphasize the role of repair processes in establishing the mutation spectra that underpin human cancer

relevance_reason: The paper studies sporadic adenocarcinoma of the small intestine. It discusses colorectal cancer only as a contrast, concluding that the small-intestinal tumours may follow a genetic pathway different from the APC-driven colorectal pathway.

findings.statement: Wheeler et al. (2002) analysed 21 non-familial, non-ampullary adenocarcinomas of the small intestine (14 male and 7 female patients; median age 64 years, range 21-85; 10 duodenal, 7 jejunal, 4 ileal). They found no mutations in the mutation cluster region of the APC gene. Only 1 tumour (5%) was replication error-positive at BAT26, and all tumours stained positive for hMLH1 and hMSH2. The authors suggested that adenocarcinoma of the small intestine may follow a different genetic pathway from colorectal cancer.
quotes: One cancer (5%) was found to be RER+, and all tumours stained positive for hMLH1 and hMSH2. No mutations were detected in the MCR of the APC gene.
We did not detect mutations in the MCR of the APC gene, and this suggests that adenocarcinoma of the small intestine may follow a different genetic pathway to colorectal cancer.
Fourteen male and seven female patients with a median age of 64 years (range 21-85) presented with adenocarcinoma of the duodenum (10), jejunum (7), and ileum (4).

findings.statement: In the 21 small-intestinal adenocarcinomas, Wheeler et al. (2002) found increased nuclear beta-catenin expression with loss of membranous staining in 10 tumours (48%). Membrane expression of E-cadherin was absent or decreased in 8 tumours (38%), and strong nuclear p53 staining was seen in 5 tumours (24%). The authors suggested that abnormal E-cadherin and beta-catenin expression reflects an early alternative to APC in this pathway.
quotes: beta-Catenin showed increased nuclear expression with loss of membranous staining in 10 cancers (48%). Absent or decreased membrane expression of E-cadherin was found in eight cancers (38%). Strong staining of p53 was found in the nucleus of five cancers (24%).
Abnormal expression of E-cadherin and beta-catenin was common and reflects an early alternative to APC in this pathway in which mutations may be found in adenocarcinoma of the small intestine.

relevance_reason: Reports somatic loss-of-function PPARG mutations in sporadic colon cancers, which supports PPARG as a somatic contributor to colorectal cancer.

findings.statement: Sarraf et al. (1999) identified 4 somatic PPAR-gamma (PPARG) mutations among 55 sporadic colon cancers: 1 nonsense, 1 frameshift, and 2 missense mutations. Each mutation greatly impaired the function of the protein. The authors concluded that colon cancer in humans is associated with loss-of-function mutations in PPARG.
quotes: We have found four somatic PPAR gamma mutations among 55 sporadic colon cancers: one nonsense, one frameshift, and two missense mutations. Each greatly impaired the function of the protein.
These data indicate that colon cancer in humans is associated with loss-of-function mutations in PPAR gamma.

findings.statement: In a sporadic colon cancer, Sarraf et al. (1999) identified a somatic frameshift mutation in PPARG, c.472delA, which results in deletion of the entire ligand-binding domain.
quotes: c.472delA results in deletion of the entire ligand binding domain.

findings.statement: In a sporadic colon cancer, Sarraf et al. (1999) identified a somatic missense mutation in PPARG, Q286P. The mutant kept the ligand-binding domain but could not activate transcription because it failed to bind ligands.
quotes: Q286P and K319X retain a total or partial ligand binding domain but lose the ability to activate transcription through a failure to bind to ligands.

findings.statement: In a sporadic colon cancer, Sarraf et al. (1999) identified a somatic nonsense mutation in PPARG, K319X. The truncated protein kept part of the ligand-binding domain but could not activate transcription because it failed to bind ligands.
quotes: Q286P and K319X retain a total or partial ligand binding domain but lose the ability to activate transcription through a failure to bind to ligands.

findings.statement: In a sporadic colon cancer, Sarraf et al. (1999) identified a somatic missense mutation in PPARG, R288H. The mutant responded normally to synthetic ligands but showed greatly decreased transcription and ligand binding when exposed to natural ligands.
quotes: R288H showed a normal response to synthetic ligands but greatly decreased transcription and binding when exposed to natural ligands.

relevance_reason: Randomized trial showing calcium supplementation reduces recurrence of colorectal adenomas (precursor lesions); relevant to clinical management/prevention of colorectal cancer.

findings.statement: Baron et al. (1999) conducted a randomized, double-blind trial in which 930 subjects (mean age 61 years; 72% men) with a recent history of colorectal adenomas received calcium carbonate (3 g, i.e. 1200 mg elemental calcium, daily) or placebo, with follow-up colonoscopies 1 and 4 years after the qualifying examination. Among the 832 subjects who completed both follow-up examinations, at least 1 adenoma was diagnosed between the first and second follow-up endoscopies in 31% of the calcium group and 38% of the placebo group (adjusted risk ratio 0.81; 95% CI 0.67-0.99; P = 0.04). The adjusted ratio of the average number of adenomas was 0.76, and the effect was independent of initial dietary fat and calcium intake. The authors concluded that calcium supplementation is associated with a significant though moderate reduction in the risk of recurrent colorectal adenomas.
quotes: We randomly assigned 930 subjects (mean age, 61 years; 72 percent men) with a recent history of colorectal adenomas to receive either calcium carbonate (3 g [1200 mg of elemental calcium] daily) or placebo, with follow-up colonoscopies one and four years after the qualifying examination.

At least one adenoma was diagnosed between the first and second follow-up endoscopies in 127 subjects in the calcium group (31 percent) and 159 subjects in the placebo group (38 percent); the adjusted risk ratio was 0.81 (95 percent confidence interval, 0.67 to 0.99; P=0.04).
Calcium supplementation is associated with a significant - though moderate - reduction in the risk of recurrent colorectal adenomas.

relevance_reason: A functional study in colorectal cancer cell lines that links DNA methylation capacity to genetic instability. It adds mechanistic context for colorectal cancer but reports no patient germline variants.

findings.statement: Lengauer et al. (1997) found striking differences in the expression of exogenously introduced retroviral genes among colorectal cancer cell lines. Loss of expression was associated with DNA methylation and could be reversed by the demethylating agent 5-azacytidine. Because genetic instability correlated strikingly with methylation capacity, the authors suggested that methylation abnormalities may play a role in chromosome segregation in cancer cells.
quotes: we report a striking difference in the expression of exogenously introduced retroviral genes in various colorectal cancer cell lines
Extinguished expression was associated with DNA methylation and could be reversed by treatment with the demethylating agent 5-azacytidine.
A striking correlation between genetic instability and methylation capacity suggested that methylation abnormalities may play a role in chromosome segregation processes in cancer cells.

findings.statement: Jones and Gonzalgo (1997) asked whether altered DNA methylation and genome instability might be a new pathway to cancer.
quotes: Altered DNA methylation and genome instability: a new pathway to cancer?

relevance_reason: Characterizes chromosomal instability versus microsatellite instability as two distinct pathways of genetic instability in colorectal cancers; pathogenesis context for the CRC entry.

findings.statement: Lengauer et al. (1997) found that colorectal tumors without microsatellite instability had a striking defect in chromosome segregation, with chromosomes gained or lost at rates above 10(-2) per chromosome per generation. This chromosomal instability reflected an ongoing cellular defect that lasted throughout the lifetime of the tumor cell and was not simply related to chromosome number.
quotes: We show here that colorectal tumours without microsatellite instability exhibit a striking defect in chromosome segregation, resulting in gains or losses in excess of 10(-2) per chromosome per generation.
This form of chromosomal instability reflected a continuing cellular defect that persisted throughout the lifetime of the tumour cell and was not simply related to chromosome number.

findings.statement: Lengauer et al. (1997) reported that microsatellite instability is a recessive trait, while chromosomal instability appeared to be dominant. They concluded that persistent genetic instability may be critical for the development of all colorectal cancers and that such instability can arise through 2 distinct pathways.
quotes: While microsatellite instability is a recessive trait, chromosomal instability appeared to be dominant.
These data indicate that persistent genetic instability may be critical for the development of all colorectal cancers, and that such instability can arise through two distinct pathways.

A theoretical paper suggesting that genomic imprinting may act as a surveillance mechanism for chromosome loss, with possible protection against cancer. It does not mention colorectal cancer specifically and reports no patients, variants or data, so it provides only general context on pathogenesis.

findings.statement: Thomas (1995) proposed that genomic imprinting could act as a surveillance mechanism for chromosome loss. Losing the transcriptionally active homologue would change gene expression, and this change could be detected. Thomas (1995) suggested that this surveillance might protect against cancer and allow monosomic and trisomic fetuses to be eliminated early.
quotes: One consequence of genomic imprinting is that loss of the transcriptionally active chromosomal homologue causes a change in gene expression that might permit surveillance of chromosome-loss events.
Possible selective advantages of such surveillance include protection against cancer and early elimination of monosomic and trisomic fetuses.

relevance_reason: Mouse model (ApcMin) study showing that reduced DNA methyltransferase activity suppresses intestinal neoplasia; relevant to the pathogenesis and animal models of colorectal cancer.

findings.statement: Laird et al. (1995) studied the effects of reduced DNA methyltransferase activity on ApcMin-induced intestinal neoplasia in mice. They combined heterozygosity for the DNA methyltransferase gene with a weekly dose of the DNA methyltransferase inhibitor 5-aza-deoxycytidine. In these treated heterozygous Min mice, the average number of intestinal adenomas fell from 113 in control mice to only 2. The authors concluded that DNA methyltransferase activity contributes substantially to tumor development in this model, and that their results argue against an oncogenic effect of DNA hypomethylation.
quotes: A reduction in the DNA methyltransferase activity in Min mice due to heterozygosity of the DNA methyltransferase gene, in conjunction with a weekly dose of the DNA methyltransferase inhibitor 5-aza-deoxycytidine, reduced the average number of intestinal adenomas from 113 in the control mice to only 2 polyps in the treated heterozygotes.
Hence, DNA methyltransferase activity contributes substantially to tumor development in this mouse model of intestinal neoplasia. Our results argue against an oncogenic effect of DNA hypomethylation.

findings.statement: Laird et al. (1995) stated that their findings in ApcMin mice are consistent with DNA methyltransferase playing a role in generating the C-to-T transitions that occur at high frequency in human colorectal tumors.
quotes: Moreover, they are consistent with a role for DNA methyltransferase in the generation of the C to T transitions seen at high frequency in human colorectal tumors.

relevance_reason: Describes a single large family with autosomal dominant inherited mucoid colon carcinoma plus extracolonic cancers (a hereditary colorectal cancer syndrome); this is useful context for the colorectal cancer entry.

findings.statement: Budd and Fink (1981) described a family in which 17 members across 3 generations had cancers. Fourteen had adenocarcinoma of the colon, mostly the mucoid variant. Other tumors in the family were endometrial adenocarcinoma, atypical endometrial hyperplasia, uterine leiomyosarcoma, transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder, and renal cell carcinoma.
quotes: Seventeen members of one family over three generations have experienced cancers, including 14 with adenocarcinoma of the colon.

producing adenocarcinoma of the endometrium, atypical endometrial hyperplasia, uterine leiomyosarcoma, and bladder transitional and renal cell carcinoma in addition to the mucoid variant of colon carcinoma.

phenotypes.hpo_label: Transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder

findings.statement: Budd and Fink (1981) concluded that the mucoid colonic carcinoma syndrome in this 3-generation family was inherited as an autosomal dominant trait. They suggested that the defective autosomal locus was pleiotropic, causing several types of extracolonic cancer.
quotes: An autosomal-dominant mucoid colonic carcinoma syndrome is described.
The defective autosomal locus is pleiotropic

relevance_reason: The paper describes a kindred with inherited colon adenocarcinoma that follows an autosomal dominant pattern, and it tests linkage to HLA. The lod score was weak and did not settle the question.

findings.statement: Sivak et al. (1981) reported a kindred with the familial cancer syndrome in which every confirmed affected member had at least one primary carcinoma of the colon. The average age at which cancer appeared was 38 years, and 23% of the cancer patients had multiple primary neoplasms. Colonoscopy found no unsuspected cancers in family members at risk.
quotes: A kindred with the familial cancer syndrome is reported in which every confirmed affected member of the pedigree had at least one primary carcinoma of the colon.
The average age at which cancer appeared was 38 years, and multiple primary neoplasm occurred in 23% of the cancer patients.
Colonoscopy eliminated the presence of any unsuspected cancers in family members at risk.

findings.statement: Sivak et al. (1981) found that transmission of the cancer trait in their colon cancer kindred was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance.
quotes: Transmission of the cancer trait is consistent with an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance.

findings.statement: Sivak et al. (1981) performed HLA typing in a kindred with inherited colon adenocarcinoma, with data from direct typing or inference available for 66 living and deceased individuals. In the offspring of 4 informative matings there were only 3 crossovers out of a possible 17, and the total lod score was 1.06 at a recombination fraction of 0.20.
quotes: HLA typing was done, and by direct typing or inference, data were available on 66 living and deceased individuals.
There were four informative matings in the kindred, the offspring of which showed only three crossovers of a possible 17.
The lod score totaled 1.06 at a recombination fraction of 0.20.

relevance_reason: Early DNA transfection study showing that a colon carcinoma cell line carries a transforming gene the same as, or closely related to, the ones in lung carcinoma lines. This is historical and molecular context for colorectal cancer.

findings.statement: Perucho et al. (1981) transfected DNA from cultured human tumor cell lines into NIH/3T3 mouse cells and looked for transformed foci. They concluded that 5 of the lines contained a gene or genes able to transform mouse cells, and that at least 3 different transforming genes were present among these 5 lines. Three of the lines, 2 from lung carcinomas and 1 from a colon carcinoma, transferred the same or closely related human genes. The authors suggested that, if these genes were mediating tumorigenesis, overlapping pathways leading to tumorigenesis may arise independently.
quotes: we conclude that five of these human tumor cell lines contain a gene or genes capable of transforming mouse cells and that at least three different transforming genes are present in these five lines
Three cell lines, two derived from lung carcinomas and one derived from a colon carcinoma, transfer the same or closely related human genes.
If these transforming genes are mediating the tumorigenic state of the human cells, then our results indicate that overlapping pathways leading to tumorigenesis may arise independently.

relevance_reason: Family study describing autosomal dominant site-specific (caecal) colon cancer without polyposis in an Indian Sikh kindred; relevant to hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer.

findings.statement: Bamezai et al. (1984) described a nonconsanguineous Indian Sikh kindred of 46 individuals in which 8 had site-specific colon (caecum) cancer not associated with polyposis. The authors considered the clinical features indicative of a 'cancer family syndrome.'
quotes: In a kindred of 46 individuals of an Indian Sikh family with no history of consanguinity, 8 suffered from site specific colon (caecum) cancer (not associated with polyposis).
The clinical features in the affected kindred were indicative of a "cancer family syndrome".

findings.statement: Bamezai et al. (1984) found that site-specific colon cancer in an Indian Sikh kindred showed an autosomal dominant transmission pattern, probably with 100% penetrance. They suggested the responsible gene may have arisen by germline mutation in the first generation and remained heterozygous in affected individuals.
quotes: The study of the family depicted an autosomal dominant transmission pattern of site specific colon cancer, with probably 100% penetrance in the affected individuals.
It is probable that the gene responsible in this family could have begun by mutation at the germ cell level in the 1st generation and remained in a heterozygous condition in the affected individuals.

findings.statement: Bamezai et al. (1984) observed a low mitotic index and no structural or numerical chromosomal aberrations in the 2 probands available for study from a kindred with site-specific colon cancer.
quotes: A low percentage of mitotic index (MI) was observed in the two probands who were available for the study. No structural or numerical chromosomal aberrations were observed in either case.

relevance_reason: Pedigree study of a large Utah kindred providing evidence for autosomal dominant inherited susceptibility to adenomatous polyps and common colorectal cancer.

findings.statement: Burt et al. (1985) studied a large Utah pedigree that had multiple cases of common colorectal cancer but no recognizable inheritance pattern. Pedigree members and spouse controls were screened with flexible proctosigmoidoscopy. One or more adenomatous polyps were found in 21% of family members (41 of 191), compared with 9% of controls (12 of 132) (P less than 0.005).
quotes: We examined the inheritance of susceptibility to colonic polyps and cancer in a large Utah pedigree with multiple cases of common colorectal cancer but no recognizable inheritance pattern among them.
One or more adenomatous polyps were found in 21 per cent of family members (41 of 191) but in only 9 per cent of controls (12 of 132) (P less than 0.005).

findings.statement: Burt et al. (1985) used likelihood methods to compare random occurrence of cancer and polyps with autosomal recessive and autosomal dominant inheritance in the Utah pedigree. The analysis suggested that the excess of discrete adenomatous polyps and colorectal cancers was caused by an inherited autosomal dominant susceptibility gene, rather than a recessive gene or chance. The authors suggested that this type of inheritance may be more common than previously recognized.
quotes: The analysis suggested that the observed excess of discrete adenomatous polyps and colorectal cancers was the result of an inherited autosomal dominant gene for susceptibility, rather than an inherited recessive gene for susceptibility or a chance occurrence.
This type of inheritance of colorectal polyps and cancer may be more common than previously recognized.

relevance_reason: Cytogenetic study implicating deletion of 12p as a specific abnormality in a limited number of colorectal carcinoma samples.

findings.statement: Pathak and Goodacre (1986) suggested that a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 12 was a specific abnormality in a limited number of colorectal carcinoma samples. They proposed that fragile sites expressed at these specific chromosomal regions in normal peripheral blood cultures might identify individuals predisposed to develop a particular type of neoplasm.
quotes: In a limited number of colorectal carcinoma samples a deletion in the short arm of a chromosome #12 is implicated as a specific abnormality.
The expression of fragile sites in these specific chromosomal regions in the normal peripheral blood cultures might identify an individual predisposed to develop a particular type of neoplasm.

relevance_reason: Reports that somatic ras (mainly KRAS codon 12) mutations are frequent in human colorectal cancers and usually occur before malignancy develops, which bears on how colorectal cancer develops.

findings.statement: Bos et al. (1987) combined DNA hybridization analyses with tissue sectioning techniques and found ras gene mutations in over a third of human colorectal cancers. Most of the mutations were at codon 12 of the c-Ki-ras (KRAS) gene.
quotes: ras gene mutations occur in over a third of human colorectal cancers, that most of the mutations are at codon 12 of the c-Ki-ras gene

findings.statement: Bos et al. (1987) concluded that ras gene mutations in colorectal tumors usually occur before malignancy develops. This suggested that they are an early event in colorectal tumor development.
quotes: the mutations usually precede the development of malignancy

relevance_reason: Reports tumor-specific loss of chromosome 5q alleles at the GRL locus in sporadic colorectal carcinomas. This supports the idea that hereditary and sporadic colon cancer involve the same 5q gene.

findings.statement: Wildrick and Boman (1988) compared matched normal and tumor DNA from patients with sporadic colon carcinoma using a probe for the glucocorticoid receptor (GRL) locus on 5q11-q13. This locus lies close to one of two proposed sites of a constitutional deletion seen in a patient with familial adenomatous polyposis. At least 27% of tumors showed tumor-specific allele loss at GRL. The authors concluded that this supports the hypothesis that hereditary and sporadic forms of colon cancer result from mutations of the same gene.
quotes: Matched normal/tumor DNA pairs from sporadic colon carcinoma patients were examined for chromosome 5 allele loss using a probe for a functional gene (glucocorticoid receptor = GRL) locus.
Tumor-specific allele loss of at least 27% at GRL supports the hypothesis that both hereditary and sporadic forms of colon cancer result from mutations of the same gene.

relevance_reason: Clonal and allelic-loss analysis of colorectal adenomas and carcinomas; shows monoclonal origin and frequent 17p loss in carcinomas, which bears on tumor progression in colorectal cancer.

findings.statement: Fearon et al. (1987) used X-linked RFLPs to study X chromosome inactivation in colorectal tumors from females. All 50 tumors examined, 20 carcinomas and 30 adenomas of either familial or spontaneous type, had monoclonal inactivation patterns. The authors concluded that this supported a monoclonal origin for colorectal neoplasms.
quotes: All 50 tumors examined showed monoclonal patterns of X chromosome inactivation; these tumors included 20 carcinomas as well as 30 adenomas of either familial or spontaneous type.
These data support a monoclonal origin for colorectal neoplasms

findings.statement: Fearon et al. (1987) used autosomal RFLPs as clonal markers. They found somatic loss of chromosome 17p sequences in more than 75% of the colorectal carcinomas examined, but such loss was rare in adenomas. The authors suggested that a gene on 17p may be associated with progression from the benign to the malignant state.
quotes: somatic loss of chromosome 17p sequences occurred in over 75 percent of the carcinomas examined, but such loss was rare in adenomas
suggest that a gene on the short arm of chromosome 17 may be associated with progression from the benign to the malignant state

relevance_reason: Reports loss of heterozygosity frequencies on chromosomes 5, 17, and 18 in sporadic colorectal carcinomas, which bears on the somatic genetics and pathogenesis of colorectal cancer.

findings.statement: Law et al. (1988) studied allelic loss in colorectal carcinomas. To get purer tumor samples, they microdissected tumor cells from 24 carcinomas, engrafted 9 more in nude mice, and flow-sorted nuclei from 2 others. Loss of heterozygosity was found for chromosome 5 alleles in 6 of 31 informative cancers (19%), for chromosome 17 in 19 of 34 (56%), and for chromosome 18 in 17 of 33 (52%).
quotes: tumor cell populations were first microdissected from 24 colorectal carcinomas, an additional nine cancers were engrafted in nude mice, and nuclei were flow-sorted from an additional two

Of 31 cancers informative for chromosome 5 markers, only 6 (19%) showed loss of heterozygosity of chromosome 5 alleles, compared to 19 of 34 (56%) on chromosome 17, and 17 of 33 (52%) on chromosome 18.

findings.statement: Law et al. (1988) concluded that the familial polyposis coli gene on chromosome 5 appears to act as a true dominant for adenomatosis but not as a common recessive gene for colon cancer. They also suggested that simple Mendelian models in which alleles are lost at a single locus may not be suitable for understanding common human solid tumors.
quotes: Therefore, it appears that (i) FPC is a true dominant for adenomatosis but not a common recessive gene for colon cancer; and (ii) simple Mendelian models involving loss of alleles at a single locus may be inappropriate for understanding common human solid tumors.

relevance_reason: Segregation/likelihood analysis supporting dominant inherited susceptibility to common colorectal adenomas and cancer.

findings.statement: Cannon-Albright et al. (1988) studied 670 persons in 34 kindreds by flexible proctosigmoidoscopy; kindreds were ascertained through a single person with an adenomatous polyp or a cluster of relatives with colon cancer, and had common colorectal cancer rather than familial polyposis coli or nonpolyposis inherited colorectal cancer. Likelihood analysis strongly supported dominant inheritance of susceptibility to colorectal adenomas and cancers, with a gene frequency of 19%. Under the most likely model, adenomatous polyps and colorectal cancers occurred only in genetically susceptible persons (95% CI for this proportion, 53 to 100%).
quotes: We studied 670 persons in 34 kindreds by flexible proctosigmoidoscopic examination (60 cm) to determine how frequently colorectal adenomas and cancers result from an inherited susceptibility.
Likelihood analysis strongly supported the dominant inheritance of a susceptibility to colorectal adenomas and cancers, with a gene frequency of 19 percent.

According to the most likely genetic model, adenomatous polyps and colorectal cancers occur only in genetically susceptible persons; however, the 95 percent confidence interval for this proportion was 53 to 100 percent.

findings.statement: Cannon-Albright et al. (1988) suggested that an inherited susceptibility to colonic adenomatous polyps and colorectal cancer is common (estimated gene frequency 19%) and is responsible for the majority of clinically observed colonic neoplasms, and that genetic and environmental factors interact in polyp formation and transformation; they supported screening of first-degree relatives of colorectal cancer patients.
quotes: These results suggest that an inherited susceptibility to colonic adenomatous polyps and colorectal cancer is common and that it is responsible for the majority of colonic neoplasms observed clinically.
The results also reinforce suggestions that first-degree relatives of patients with colorectal cancer should be screened for colonic tumors.

relevance_reason: Landmark study of somatic genetic alterations (ras mutations, 5q, 17p, 18q loss) across stages of colorectal tumor development, establishing the multistep model of colorectal tumorigenesis.

findings.statement: Vogelstein et al. (1988) looked for ras-gene mutations and allelic deletions of chromosomes 5, 17, and 18 in 172 colorectal tumor specimens representing different stages of neoplasia: 40 predominantly early-stage adenomas from 7 patients with familial adenomatous polyposis, 40 adenomas from 33 patients without polyposis, and 92 carcinomas from 89 patients. Ras-gene mutations occurred in 58% of adenomas larger than 1 cm and 47% of carcinomas, but in only 9% of adenomas under 1 cm.
quotes: We looked for four genetic alterations (ras-gene mutations and allelic deletions of chromosomes 5, 17, and 18) in 172 colorectal-tumor specimens representing various stages of neoplastic development.

We found that ras-gene mutations occurred in 58 percent of adenomas larger than 1 cm and in 47 percent of carcinomas. However, ras mutations were found in only 9 percent of adenomas under 1 cm in size.

findings.statement: Vogelstein et al. (1988) found that chromosome 5 sequences linked to the familial adenomatous polyposis gene were not lost in adenomas from polyposis patients but were lost in 29 to 35% of adenomas and carcinomas from other patients. A specific region of chromosome 18 was deleted in 73% of carcinomas and 47% of advanced adenomas but in only 11 to 13% of earlier-stage adenomas, and chromosome 17p sequences were usually lost only in carcinomas (75%).
quotes: Sequences on chromosome 5 that are linked to the gene for familial adenomatous polyposis were not lost in adenomas from the patients with polyposis but were lost in 29 to 35 percent of adenomas and carcinomas, respectively, from other patients.
A specific region of chromosome 18 was deleted frequently in carcinomas (73 percent) and in advanced adenomas (47 percent) but only occasionally in earlier-stage adenomas (11 to 13 percent).
Chromosome 17p sequences were usually lost only in carcinomas (75 percent).

findings.statement: Vogelstein et al. (1988) found that the four molecular alterations accumulated in a fashion paralleling the clinical progression of colorectal tumors, consistent with a model in which development of cancer often involves mutational activation of an oncogene coupled with loss of several tumor suppressor genes.
quotes: The four molecular alterations accumulated in a fashion that paralleled the clinical progression of tumors.

These results are consistent with a model of colorectal tumorigenesis in which the steps required for the development of cancer often involve the mutational activation of an oncogene coupled with the loss of several genes that normally suppress tumorigenesis.

relevance_reason: Loss-of-heterozygosity study of familial polyposis and sporadic colorectal carcinomas. It implicates several chromosomal loci, including chromosome 22 and the FPC-linked 5q region, in colon carcinoma development.

findings.statement: Okamoto et al. (1988) used polymorphic DNA markers to look for somatic loss of heterozygosity in 38 tumors from 25 patients with familial polyposis coli and in 20 sporadic colon carcinomas from 19 patients. Allele loss on chromosome 22 was frequent, with some additional losses on chromosomes 5, 6, 12q, and 15. The authors suggested that more than one chromosomal locus may be involved in the development of familial and sporadic colon carcinomas.
quotes: Investigation of 38 tumours from 25 FPC patients, and 20 sporadic colon carcinomas from 19 patients, revealed frequent occurrence of allele loss on chromosome 22, with some additional losses on chromosomes 5, 6, 12q and 15.
These results suggest the possible involvement of more than one chromosomal locus in the development of familial and sporadic colon carcinomas.

findings.statement: Okamoto et al. (1988) found frequent allele loss with C11p11, a DNA probe linked to the familial polyposis coli gene, in both familial and sporadic colon carcinomas. They did not find this loss in benign adenomas.
quotes: The FPC gene-linked DNA probe C11p11 also detected frequent allele loss in both familial and sporadic colon carcinomas but not in benign adenomas.

relevance_reason: Population-based study estimating the frequency of hereditary colorectal cancer (cancer family syndrome/HNPCC, familial adenomatosis) among all colorectal carcinoma patients in a Finnish county.

findings.statement: Mecklin (1987) studied all 468 colorectal carcinoma patients diagnosed in one Finnish county (0.25 million inhabitants) from 1970 to 1979 and found that the cancer family syndrome type of hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal carcinoma was the most common verifiable risk factor, involving 3.8 to 5.5% of patients. The frequencies of familial adenomatosis and ulcerative colitis were 0.2% and 0.6%, respectively. Because diagnosis relied on family history with cancer in 2 or more generations, the author suggested that the observed frequency of 4 to 6% for the syndrome may be an underestimate.
quotes: The frequency of hereditary colorectal carcinoma was evaluated in a study group consisting of all colorectal carcinoma patients (n = 468) diagnosed in one Finnish county (0.25 million inhabitants) during the period 1970-1979.

The cancer family syndrome type of hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal carcinoma emerged as the most common verifiable risk factor for colon cancer involving 3.8%-5.5% of all colorectal carcinoma patients in this study. The frequencies of familial adenomatosis and ulcerative colitis were 0.2% and 0.6%, respectively.
The cancer family syndrome cannot be diagnosed on the basis of a single patient, and so the observed frequency of 4%-6% for the syndrome may still represent an underestimate.

findings.statement: Mecklin (1987) found that patients with cancer family syndrome were young, accounting for 29 to 39% of colorectal carcinoma patients under 50 years of age, and that their tumors were located predominantly (65%) in the right hemicolon. The author concluded that the high frequency of hereditary cases indicated the importance of taking the family history of every new patient.
quotes: The patients with cancer family syndrome were young, accounting for 29%-39% of the patients under 50 yr of age, and their tumors were located predominantly (65%) in the right hemicolon.
The high frequency of hereditary cases among colorectal carcinoma patients indicates the importance of studying the family history of every new patient.

relevance_reason: Somatic genetic alterations (ras mutations, chromosome 5/17/18 deletions, aneuploidy) in colorectal tumors, comparing proximal vs distal sites.

findings.statement: Delattre et al. (1989) investigated multiple genetic alterations in colorectal cancers, including changes in DNA content, ras oncogene mutations, and deletions involving chromosomes 5, 17, and 18. Deletions and mitotic abnormalities were both significantly more frequent in distal than in proximal tumors, and deletions were significantly associated with each other and with change in DNA content.
quotes: Multiple genetic alterations were investigated in colorectal cancer, including changes in DNA content, mutations in ras oncogenes, and deletions involving chromosomes 5, 17, and 18.
A non-random association of deletions and mitotic abnormalities by site was seen, with both types of alterations occurring significantly more frequently in distal tumours.
In addition, deletions were significantly associated with each other and with change in DNA content.

findings.statement: Delattre et al. (1989) found that the frequency of somatic c-Ki-ras mutations in colorectal cancer did not differ between proximal and distal tumors.
quotes: In contrast, the frequency of c-Ki-ras mutations did not differ between proximal and distal cancers.

findings.statement: Delattre et al. (1989) concluded that their data strongly supported the hypothesis that proximal and distal colon carcinomas might differ in the genetic mechanisms underlying their initiation and/or progression.
quotes: The data provide strong support for the hypothesis that proximal and distal colon carcinoma might differ in the genetic mechanisms in their initiation and/or progression.

relevance_reason: Genome-wide allelic loss (LOH) study of 56 colorectal carcinomas, with a correlation between allelic deletions and prognosis; somatic genetic evidence relevant to colorectal cancer.

findings.statement: Vogelstein et al. (1989) studied polymorphic DNA markers from every nonacrocentric autosomal arm in 56 paired colorectal carcinoma and adjacent normal colonic mucosa specimens. They called this analysis an 'allelotype.' Allelic deletions were very common: for every polymorphic marker tested, one allele was lost in at least some tumors, and some tumors lost more than half of their parental alleles.
quotes: polymorphic DNA markers were studied from every nonacrocentric autosomal arm in 56 paired colorectal carcinoma and adjacent normal colonic mucosa specimens
Allelic deletions were remarkably common; one of the alleles of each polymorphic marker tested was lost in at least some tumors, and some tumors lost more than half of their parental alleles.

findings.statement: Vogelstein et al. (1989) found new DNA fragments that were absent from normal tissue in 5 of 56 colorectal carcinomas. These new fragments contained repeated sequences of the variable number of tandem repeat (VNTR) type.
quotes: new DNA fragments not present in normal tissue were identified in five carcinomas; these new fragments contained repeated sequences of the variable number of tandem repeat type

findings.statement: Vogelstein et al. (1989) found that patients whose colorectal carcinomas had more than the median percentage of allelic deletions had a considerably worse prognosis than the other patients, even though primary tumor size and stage were very similar in the two groups. The authors suggested that tumor allelotype may provide a molecular tool for better estimating prognosis in colorectal cancer.
quotes: Patients with more than the median percentage of allelic deletions had a considerably worse prognosis than did the other patients, although the size and stage of the primary tumors were very similar in the two groups.
tumor allelotype may provide a molecular tool for improved estimation of prognosis in patients with colorectal cancer

relevance_reason: Only the title is available. It shows that the paper proposes a genetic model of how colorectal tumors develop, which bears on the pathogenesis of colorectal cancer. No patients, genes or variants can be taken from the title.

findings.statement: Fearon and Vogelstein (1990) proposed a genetic model for colorectal tumorigenesis.
quotes: A genetic model for colorectal tumorigenesis.

relevance_reason: Cytogenetic study of 15 colorectal adenocarcinomas reporting recurrent chromosomal losses/gains (17p, 18, 9q, sex chromosomes), relevant to the cytogenetics section of the colorectal cancer entry.

findings.statement: Konstantinova et al. (1991) analyzed chromosome abnormalities in 15 colorectal tumors. Rearrangements of 17p leading to deletion of the arm or part of it were found in 12 tumors, and loss of one chromosome 17 homolog in 2 others; loss of chromosome 18 was found in 12 of 13 cases with fully identified numerical abnormalities. Other losses involved chromosome 5 (6 tumors), 21 (5), and 4, 15, and 22 (4 each); gains included extra copies of chromosome 20 (6 tumors), 8q (5), and 13q (6), and rearrangements of 1p and 11q were each found in 6 tumors.
quotes: Rearrangements of the short arm of chromosome 17, leading to deletions of this arm or its part were noted in 12 tumors; in 2 other cases, one of the homologs of pair 17 was lost.
chromosome 18, in 12 out of 13 cases with fully identified numerical abnormalities; chromosome 5, in 6 tumors; chromosome 21, in 5 cases; chromosomes 4, 15, and 22, in 4 cases each.
Additional homologs of pair 20 were observed in 6 tumors, extra 8q was found in 5 tumors, and extra 13q in 6 cases.

findings.statement: Konstantinova et al. (1991) noted that, unlike other series, their colorectal tumors showed a high frequency of sex chromosome loss (X missing in 4 of 7 tumors from females; Y absent in 5 of 8 tumors from males) and rearrangements of 9q in 8 cases, with the breakpoint at 9q22 in 5. Cytologic signs of gene amplification (double minutes or multiple microchromosomes) were seen in 6 tumors.
quotes: X chromosomes were missing in 4 out of 7 tumors in females, and Y chromosomes were absent in 5 out of 8 tumors in males.
The long arm of chromosome 9 was rearranged in 8 cases, in 5 of them the breakpoint being at 9q22.
Cytological manifestations of gene amplification (double minutes or multiple microchromosomes) were noted in 6 tumors.

relevance_reason: A population-based segregation analysis of colorectal cancer families. It supports dominant transmission of susceptibility with reduced penetrance.

findings.statement: Ponz de Leon et al. (1992) performed classical segregation analysis on 605 families of colorectal carcinoma probands ascertained through the Cancer Registry of the Province of Modena, Italy. Of these, 28 were suspected HNPCC families and 577 were presumed non-HNPCC. Among the non-HNPCC families, both parents were affected in 11, one parent in 130 and neither parent in 436. In the suspected HNPCC families, segregation was compatible with dominant transmission of susceptibility to carcinoma.
quotes: Classical segregation analysis was conducted on 605 families of probands with colorectal carcinoma ascertained through the Cancer Registry of the Province of Modena in Italy.
The families were classified as 28 suspected hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC) syndromes and 577 presumed non-HNPCC.
In the suspected HNPCC families, segregation was compatible with dominant transmission of susceptibility to carcinoma.

findings.statement: Ponz de Leon et al. (1992) found that in colorectal cancer families with one affected parent, the segregation frequency was almost exactly equal to that in families where both parents were normal. A model of dominant transmission of susceptibility through a major gene with greatly reduced penetrance in heterozygotes fitted the data acceptably.
quotes: In families with one parent affected, the segregation frequency was almost exactly equal to the frequency of segregation in families where both parents were normal.
The model of dominant transmission of susceptibility through a major gene with greatly reduced penetrance in heterozygotes fitted the data acceptably.

relevance_reason: Complex segregation analysis providing evidence for dominant susceptibility genes for colorectal cancer, with estimates of gene frequency and penetrance.

findings.statement: Houlston et al. (1992) performed complex segregation analysis of a published series of consecutive pedigrees ascertained through patients treated for colorectal cancer. The analysis favored a dominant gene or genes with a frequency of 0.006 and a lifetime penetrance of 0.63.
quotes: The genetic basis for colorectal cancer was investigated by complex segregation analysis of a published series of consecutive pedigrees ascertained through patients undergoing treatment for colorectal cancer.
Analysis favoured a dominant gene or genes with a frequency of 0.006 with a lifetime penetrance of 0.63.

findings.statement: Houlston et al. (1992) estimated that these dominant genes accounted for 81% of colorectal cancer in patients under 35 years of age, whereas by age 65 about 85% of cases were phenocopies.
quotes: These genes account for 81% of colorectal cancer in patients under 35, however, by 65 about 85% are phenocopies.

relevance_reason: Somatic TP53 mutation and LOH analysis in colorectal tumors of different grades shows that changes in both p53 alleles go along with the move from adenoma to early carcinoma. This is relevant to colorectal cancer pathogenesis.

findings.statement: Kikuchi-Yanoshita et al. (1992) looked for p53 mutations and loss of heterozygosity (LOH) in 274 colorectal tumors of 4 histopathologic grades. In 160 tumors from 40 patients with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), p53 mutations were found in 0 of 58 adenomas with moderate dysplasia, 3 of 37 severe adenomas, 6 of 40 intramucosal carcinomas, and 10 of 25 invasive carcinomas. Both mutation and LOH were seen in 1 of 33 severe adenomas, 6 of 24 intramucosal carcinomas, and 10 of 25 invasive carcinomas. Every intramucosal and invasive carcinoma with a mutation had lost the other p53 allele.
quotes: Among 160 tumors from 40 familial adenomatous polyposis patients, none of 58 adenomas with moderate dysplasia had p53 mutations, whereas 8% (3 of 37) of severe adenomas, 15% (6 of 40) of intramucosal carcinomas, and 40% (10 of 25) of invasive carcinomas had p53 mutations.
Only 3% (1 of 33) of severe adenomas showed both mutation and LOH, while 25% (6 of 24) of intramucosal carcinomas and 40% (10 of 25) of invasive carcinomas had both mutation and LOH.
All intramucosal and invasive carcinomas that had mutations lost the other allele of the p53 gene.

findings.statement: Kikuchi-Yanoshita et al. (1992) obtained similar results in 114 tumors from 86 patients without FAP. No adenoma had both a p53 mutation and LOH, but both changes were present in intramucosal and invasive carcinomas.
quotes: In 114 tumors from 86 non-familial adenomatous polyposis patients, similar results were obtained; no adenoma showed both mutation and LOH, but both alterations occurred in intramucosal and invasive carcinoma.

findings.statement: Of the 56 p53 mutations that Kikuchi-Yanoshita et al. (1992) found, the codons most often affected were 175, 238, 245, 248, 273, and 282; 4 of these codons encode arginine. GC-to-AT transitions made up 39 of 54 mutations (72%).
quotes: the frequently affected codons were codons 175, 238, 245, 248, 273, and 282, 4 of these amino acids being arginine, and 72% (39 of 54) of all mutations were GC to AT transition.

findings.statement: Kikuchi-Yanoshita et al. (1992) found high p53 polyadenylated RNA expression in every invasive carcinoma, whether or not a mutation or LOH was present. p53 protein immunostaining was negative in almost all adenomas but positive in 86% of invasive carcinomas with a p53 mutation. The authors suggested that changes in both p53 alleles through mutation and LOH, leading to abnormal protein accumulation, are involved in the conversion of adenoma to early carcinoma.
quotes: immunostaining of p53 protein was negative in almost all adenomas, but it was positive in 86% of invasive carcinomas exhibiting p53 mutation.

These data suggest that genetic changes on both alleles of the p53 gene through mutation and LOH, which result in abnormal protein accumulation, are involved in the conversion of adenoma to early carcinoma.

relevance_reason: Describes a family with familial early-onset gastrointestinal carcinoma across four generations; adds family evidence for hereditary colorectal/GI cancer (abstract only).

findings.statement: Lovett (1976) described a family with a high incidence of early-onset gastrointestinal carcinoma, with affected individuals proven in four generations. The management of unaffected family members was discussed and a follow-up regimen was suggested.
quotes: A family with a high incidence of early onset gastrointestinal carcinoma is described. Individuals from four generations have been proved to have had the disease.
The management of individuals as yet unaffected is discussed and a regime for follow-up suggested.

relevance_reason: Family study of 209 patients with colorectal cancer that showed familial aggregation and features of the index case that predict familial risk.

findings.statement: Lovett (1976) took family histories from 209 patients being treated for cancer of the colon or rectum at St Mark's Hospital and obtained death certificates for parents and sibs who had died. Among these relatives, deaths from bowel cancer were more than three times the number expected for a comparable group from the general population.
quotes: Family histories were obtained from 209 patients undergoing treatment for cancer of the colon or rectum at St Mark's Hospital.
Among these, the number of deaths from cancer of the bowel was more than three times that expected for a comparable group from the general population.

phenotypes.text: cancer of the colon or rectum

findings.statement: Lovett (1976) identified three features of an index case that were associated with a higher likelihood that other family members had also had cancer of the large bowel: multiple benign or malignant tumors in the large bowel, a history of a previous primary carcinoma or adenoma of the large bowel, and early age of onset of bowel carcinoma.
quotes: These are, first, the presence of multiple benign or malignant tumours in the large bowel, secondly, a history of previous primary carcinoma or adenoma of the large bowel and, thirdly, early age of onset of carcinoma of the bowel.

phenotypes.text: multiple benign or malignant tumours in the large bowel
previous primary carcinoma or adenoma of the large bowel
early age of onset of carcinoma of the bowel

relevance_reason: Abstract describes another 'cancer family' (hereditary colon/uterine cancer) and recommends screening for colon and uterine cancer; this is clinical-management context for familial colorectal cancer.

findings.statement: Williams (1978) described a further 'cancer family' and recommended that cancer patients from such families receive careful lifelong follow-up. Williams (1978) also recommended that all members of cancer families be screened for cancer of the uterus and colon and be taught methods of cancer detection and the importance of early diagnosis.
quotes: A further "cancer family" is described. Cancer patients from such a family require careful lifelong follow-up.
All members of cancer families should be screened for cancer of the uterus and colon, and they should be educated in methods of cancer detection and the importance of early diagnosis.
